narrate.summary: This paper derives reliability expressions for a one-out-of-n cold standby system whose active components follow a Generalized Lindley distribution (GLD). It models component lifetimes as identically distributed and derives the distribution of their sum using a moment-generating-function approach. With a perfect switch, it gives a closed-form system reliability expression; with an imperfect switch, it gives a lower bound because exact calculations are described as difficult. The numerical illustration considers a 100-hour mission and systems with 2, 5, 10, and 20 components, using specified distribution parameters rather than measured lifetime data. In that illustration, imperfect switching reduces reliability relative to perfect switching, while adding components increases reliability, especially with a perfect switch.
narrate.key_results: The authors derive a closed-form reliability expression and a mean time to failure formula for the perfect-switch system, and a lower bound for the imperfect-switch system. The numerical illustration uses 2, 5, 10, and 20 components over a 100-hour mission; the plotted results show lower reliability with the imperfect switch and higher reliability as component count increases, particularly for the perfect switch. Sensitivity analysis identifies theta as having the greatest influence on reliability, while eta and gamma have the least influence. For the reported mean-time-to-failure sensitivity with respect to alpha, the values for 2, 5, 10, and 20 components are 3.4932, 8.7329, 17.4658, and 34.9317, respectively; the corresponding values for beta are 0.5068, 1.2671, 2.5342, and 5.0683.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The analysis assumes identical component lifetime distributions and the usual cold-standby conditions, including healthy standby components and negligible switching time, so it does not represent heterogeneity or non-negligible transition delays. narrate.summary: This paper estimates relative variability in lifetimes when failures are observed only within scheduled time intervals and some surviving units are withdrawn during the study. It models lifetimes with a two-parameter Weibull distribution and estimates the Pearson and second-order coefficients of variation. The methods include maximum likelihood, linear and nonlinear least squares, and Bayesian estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation; the authors also construct confidence and credible intervals. They evaluate the methods in simulations with several sample sizes, monitoring schedules, censoring schemes, and parameter settings, and apply them to survival data from 112 patients with plasma cell myeloma. The authors report that Bayesian estimation with informative gamma priors and the proposed least-squares methods perform well for point estimation, while highest posterior density intervals often have the strongest coverage.
narrate.key_results: The simulation study used 1,000 replications, sample sizes of 50 and 200, and four or eight examination points. For shape 1.25, rate 0.052, scheme I, sample size 200, and eight examination points, the reported mean squared error for the Pearson coefficient was 0.0054 for Bayesian estimation, compared with 0.0058 for maximum likelihood, 0.0063 for linear least squares, and 0.0059 for nonlinear least squares. For the same setting, the second-order coefficient’s mean squared errors were 0.0011, 0.0012, 0.0014, and 0.0014, respectively. In many simulated settings, the highest posterior density intervals had coverage near or above the nominal 95 percent; for example, their reported coverage for the Pearson coefficient was 0.987 in one setting with shape 0.75, rate 0.052, scheme I, sample size 50, and four examination points. In the patient dataset, the Pearson coefficient point estimates ranged from 0.8141 to 0.8261 across the four estimation approaches, and the linear least-squares bootstrap interval had width 0.2552, the narrowest reported interval for that coefficient.

narrate.summary: The paper derives a conservative Bayesian method for assessing on-demand software reliability when an assessor specifies only partial prior beliefs about the probability of failure on demand (pfd). It models demand outcomes as an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Bernoulli process and finds the least favorable posterior predictive probability that the software will operate correctly on future demands. The method uses prior probabilities assigned to intervals of possible failure probabilities and reduces the assessment to a finite optimization with a unique fixed-point solution. The authors illustrate the method numerically by comparing its required test demands with those obtained using a uniform prior. The paper is theoretical and uses no field or other empirical data.
narrate.key_results: The authors show that the conservative solution is determined by a unique fixed point and that its prior places probability mass at selected interval endpoints and fixed-point locations. In the table’s example with no observed failures, a uniform prior requires 4,602 demands for each of three future-reliability claims, while the conservative method with y2 equal to 10^-4 requires 46,861, 49,322, and 51,882 demands, respectively. With one observed failure, the corresponding uniform-prior requirements are 9,229, 9,450, and 9,681 demands, compared with 52,320, 54,417, and 56,634 under that conservative prior specification. The authors also find that the conservative-to-uniform testing gap is roughly an order of magnitude for the small failure counts shown, and that the conservative solution increases with observed successes and decreases with observed failures.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses nonuniform etched thickness and uncertainty in plasma etching, where wafer-to-wafer process settings and spatial variation affect whether the remaining oxide thickness meets its target. It models mean thickness and input-dependent spatial variability separately using a heteroscedastic Gaussian process, while also representing uncertainty from sparse training data. The model and reliability-based design optimization framework use 84 laboratory experimental input-output runs, each with thickness measured at nine wafer locations. The optimization searches for process settings that reduce thickness variance while meeting a specified probability-of-failure requirement. For the illustrated target, accounting for model uncertainty produced a design with a lower reported failure probability than optimization that considered only process variability, at the cost of a slightly higher variance.
narrate.key_results: Across 10 random training and test splits, the heteroscedastic Gaussian process had a mean-thickness root mean square error of 1.5749 ± 0.3249, identical to the standard Gaussian process, but its variance-prediction error was 0.4005 ± 0.1457 versus 17.1884 ± 4.1281 for the standard model. Its continuous ranked probability score was 1.1150 ± 0.1558 versus 1.3410 ± 0.1018, and its conditional negative log-likelihood was 1.3843 ± 0.1239 versus 2.4019 ± 0.0941. For a 240 nm target, ±2.4 nm tolerance, and 3.0% target failure probability, the aleatory-only design had variance 0.9136 nm² and failure probability 2.94%; the design accounting for aleatory and epistemic uncertainty had variance 0.9626 nm² and failure probability 0.71%. In the most stringent scenario, the aleatory-only method reported a design with 1.52% failure probability against a 1.5% target, whereas the method accounting for both uncertainty types found no feasible solution.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an adaptive Bayesian reliability acceptance sampling plan using simple step-stress partial accelerated life testing for products with multiple competing failure causes. Units start at normal stress, and stress is raised at a preset time only if the number of early failures is below a chosen threshold; testing ends after a fixed number of failures. The method assumes independent exponential failure times for each cause, uses the cumulative exposure model, and accounts for sampling, test duration, salvage, rejection, and elevated-stress costs. The authors derive a Bayes decision rule and optimize sample size, failure count, early-failure threshold, and, when not fixed, stress-change time to minimize expected loss. They illustrate the method with numerical comparisons, simulated data, and laboratory life-test data for solar lighting devices with capacitor and controller failures.
narrate.key_results: In the numerical example, the adaptive plan had expected risk 35.964 compared with 36.582 for the conventional non-accelerated plan, a reported relative risk saving of 1.718%; the accelerated plan had the same risk as the adaptive plan in that scenario. Across the reported parameter scenarios, the largest relative risk saving over the non-accelerated plan was 2.526%. For the solar-device example with the stress-change time fixed at 5 hundred hours, the selected adaptive design used 7 units and stopped at 5 failures, with risk 77.126; the reported risks were 77.283 for the accelerated plan and 77.236 for the non-accelerated plan. The paper also reports that the fitted parametric reliability curves were close to the nonparametric curves for both failure causes and the whole unit in this dataset.

narrate.summary: This tutorial explains how progressive wear or performance loss can lead to a soft failure when a measured characteristic crosses a chosen threshold. It introduces general path models and stochastic process models for describing degradation, estimating failure-time distributions, and predicting remaining useful life. The paper discusses repeated measurements on the same units and destructive tests that measure different units at different times, using laboratory and field examples such as lasers, coatings, adhesive bonds, metal fatigue, and road sections. It also covers accelerated testing, time-varying environmental conditions, software, and applications in several industries. The authors recommend general path models in most practical cases while cautioning that predictions beyond the observed data can be unreliable.
narrate.key_results: The paper is a tutorial and does not report a single head-to-head performance study or an overall accuracy measure. In the adhesive-bond example, the parametric and semiparametric methods give thermal-index estimates of 33 and 34 degrees Celsius, respectively, compared with 39 degrees Celsius from the traditional method; the authors report that they recommend the former two methods over the traditional method. In the road-section example, sequentially adding individual observations reduces uncertainty in predicted remaining useful life, but the paper gives no numerical measure of that improvement. The tutorial also reports examples including 15 laser units and a coating study with 48 samples tested under 12 conditions.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors limit the tutorial to general path and stochastic process models for repeated-measures and accelerated destructive test data, although they note that other forms of degradation data may require other methods. They caution that extrapolation over time or to other accelerating conditions can be inaccurate even when a model fits the observed data, and recommend sensitivity analysis. They also note that stochastic process models can be biased when the mean trend is misspecified and can be less flexible for nonlinear trends, dynamic covariates, and destructive-test data.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper does not conduct a common, systematic comparison of the reviewed approaches on shared data, so readers cannot infer general accuracy rankings from the case examples. Several examples are drawn from previously published studies, and the tutorial does not provide prospective field validation of predictions made from accelerated tests. Results also depend on choices such as the failure threshold and model assumptions about measurement error, dependence, and unit-to-unit variation.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify multivariate and functional degradation data, sensor-based methods, and Bayesian and machine-learning approaches as active directions. They advocate physics-informed machine learning to address concerns about prediction and extrapolation, and expect modeling degradation in artificial intelligence systems to become an important research area.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the reviewed models using shared field datasets, prespecified failure thresholds, and prospective prediction tests, including explicit evaluation of extrapolation from accelerated conditions. narrate.summary: The paper addresses reliability analysis when a computer simulator can produce different outputs under the same input conditions, making direct failure-probability estimation computationally expensive. It proposes active learning stochastic polynomial chaos expansions (AL-SPCE), which trains stochastic polynomial chaos expansion (SPCE) surrogates with new evaluations directed toward input regions that are both important to failure probability and uncertain. The method estimates conditional failure probabilities and uses the spread of surrogate predictions, derived from maximum-likelihood coefficient uncertainty, to guide sampling. It is tested on a resistance-load example, a stochastic infectious-disease outbreak model, and a simulated wind-turbine dataset. Across these studies, the active strategy generally gives more stable and efficient estimates than fixed-design surrogates or direct Monte Carlo simulation, although some bias and noisy convergence remain.
narrate.key_results: In the resistance-load example, the reference failure probability is 3.154 × 10^-3; with 50 training points, AL-SPCE has a median estimate of 3.052 × 10^-3 and a 33.6% coefficient of variation, compared with 3.748 × 10^-3 and 52.0% for the fixed design. For the outbreak model, the reference is 7.511 × 10^-4; at 2,000 points, the active method gives 6.929 × 10^-4 with a 4.5% coefficient of variation, while the fixed design gives 1.464 × 10^-3 with a 26.8% coefficient of variation and direct Monte Carlo simulation gives 5.000 × 10^-4 with a 75.4% coefficient of variation. For the wind-turbine dataset, the reference is 2.031 × 10^-3; at 1,000 points, the active estimate is 1.798 × 10^-3, compared with 5.127 × 10^-3 for the fixed design and 2.000 × 10^-3 for direct Monte Carlo simulation. Results are based on 15 repeated runs per case; the paper reports that useful estimates can often be obtained with substantially fewer model evaluations than the alternatives, but the outbreak estimates show persistent underestimation at the tested sample sizes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that a robust stopping criterion remains unresolved because the convergence curves are noisy, partly due to simulator randomness and partly due to the optimization used to train the surrogate. They note that applicability is constrained by the scalability of SPCE, estimating that it handles roughly 10 to 20 input variables without dimensionality-reduction methods for higher dimensions. They also did not compare the method with other advanced reliability methods for stochastic simulators.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported validation uses simulated examples and a simulated wind-turbine dataset, not independent physical field measurements, so performance on operational data is not established. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify a more robust stopping criterion as an open need. They propose reformulating SPCE in a Bayesian setting, which could provide built-in local uncertainty estimates and meaningful regularization.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The method could be tested against physical wind-turbine operating records and other field datasets, including validation under changing operating conditions. narrate.summary: The paper addresses how to choose stress levels and allocate test units in constant-stress accelerated life testing when the goal is to predict lifetime at normal operating conditions. It models time to failure with Weibull accelerated failure time models and optimizes plans by simulating censored test data and minimizing prediction error. The authors examine simulated data for linear, quadratic, and power-law relationships, as well as laboratory accelerated-test data for electronic components. Their results favor two stress levels for the linear and power-law examples and three for the quadratic examples, with more units generally assigned to lower stresses. The framework is presented as a flexible alternative to analytical design optimization, particularly for plans with many design points or practical constraints.
narrate.key_results: For the simulated linear case with 100 test units, the two-stress plan used stress levels 0.19 and 0.89, allocated 85 and 15 units, and had a mean RMSE of 7,038. For the simulated quadratic case, the authors favor a three-stress plan at 0.13, about 0.5, and 0.90, allocating 66, 27, and 7 units; its reported mean RMSE was 9,004, while other tested plans had similar error. In the electronic-component study, the selected quadratic model received 99.97% of the AIC weight, and the favored plan used approximately 2.9, 4, and 5 kilovolts with allocations of about 80, 60, and 20 units; its mean RMSE was 37,107. In that same case study, alternative model extrapolations to the 2.1-kilovolt design stress gave estimated lifetimes of approximately 5, 44, and 276 years for the linear, quadratic, and power-law models, respectively.

narrate.summary: This paper tests whether ChatGPT can generate MATLAB code for reliability analysis, an important task that can be difficult for engineers without programming or probability expertise. The authors use zero-shot prompts to generate code for the first-order reliability method (FORM), subset simulation, random-field generation, and Bayesian updating with Gibbs sampling. They test the code on simulated examples and compare outputs with established methods, including Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) and independent implementations. Some generated programs produce close benchmark results, but other attempts fail or require revised prompts. The main conclusion is that code generation can speed up reliability programming, but expert checking is still needed.

For subset simulation, the reported circular and parabolic examples gave failure probabilities of 3.14 × 10^-4 versus 3.36 × 10^-4, and 2.35 × 10^-3 versus 2.36 × 10^-3, respectively, when compared with MCS. The random-field examples reproduced the prescribed directional correlation lengths reasonably well in comparison with benchmark results. For five-dimensional Bayesian updating, the estimated parameters agreed closely with the simulated population values, and missing-value estimates were reported as almost similar to those from an independent method.

The region is chosen to maximize expected utility, defined as economic benefit minus expected warranty cost. The combined policy on both dimensions gave the largest reported utility at each of the three sale prices: 191.9923 at 500, 189.7210 at 700, and 187.658 at 900. narrate.summary: Infrequent inspections by a Track Recording Car (TRC) leave increasing uncertainty in forecasts of track geometry, while lower-cost on-board sensors provide more frequent but noisier measurements. The paper models track degradation with a multivariate Wiener process and combines its forecasts with sensor indices using a Kalman filter. The method is evaluated using a year of data from Queensland, Australia, where low-cost sensors were mounted on a TRC, and with Monte Carlo simulations of different sensor recording intervals. The study considers longitudinal Top and Alignment indicators, and finds that adding sensor observations reduces prediction uncertainty compared with using the degradation model alone. The authors also examine how measurement frequency affects the width and stability of prediction credibility zones.
narrate.key_results: At a 3-month prediction horizon, weekly sensor measurements reduced credibility-interval width by about 55–70% for Top and 20–50% for Alignment, compared with predictions without on-board data. With measurements every 4 weeks, the reported reductions at that horizon were typically 40–60% for Top and 15–40% for Alignment. At 6 months, weekly measurements reduced width by up to 80–90% for Top and 40–60% for Alignment in fast-degradation cases; for typical and slow cases, reductions were generally 50–75% for Top and 30–55% for Alignment. The authors report that even 4-week measurements reduced long-term uncertainty by more than 40% in many cases, and that shorter intervals brought credibility zones to a stable level sooner.

narrate.summary: This paper addresses the shortage of run-to-failure data for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, while recognizing that airlines may not want to share sensor data. It presents a federated learning (FL) framework in which airline clients train a shared neural network and validate models using local validation data, sharing losses rather than data. The method is tested with six training engines and three test engines from the N-CMAPSS aircraft-engine dataset, with additional simulated sensor noise applied to two training engines. The shared model performs better than separate airline models for five of the six clients, and the proposed aggregation methods can reduce the effect of noisy client data, particularly at higher noise levels.
narrate.key_results: The FL model had an overall root mean squared error (RMSE) of 9.9 flights on the three test engines, compared with a mean RMSE of 15.8 flights across the six separately trained models; it performed better than five of those six models. The centralized model, which uses all training data, had an overall RMSE of 6.3 flights. With no added noise, standard data-size-weighted averaging had an RMSE of 9.9 flights, while the proposed aggregation methods ranged from 10.1 to 12.2 flights. When noise with a standard deviation multiplier of 1 was added to two clients' data, the Full-Best method achieved an RMSE of 9.5 flights, compared with 12.3 flights for standard averaging.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses only six training engines and three test engines from one benchmark dataset, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of aircraft fleets, operators, and failure patterns. narrate.summary: The paper addresses how crystallographic texture variability in welded 316L stainless steel affects stress and strain responses associated with degradation precursors such as strain localization and crack initiation. It combines crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) simulations with a polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) surrogate to reduce the computational burden of uncertainty analysis. The inputs come from electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) maps of electron-beam-welded material, while the mechanical responses come from simulations calibrated against experimental stress-strain data. The study selects a representative volume element (RVE) with about 615 grains and trains the surrogate using 200 simulations. The work estimates stress variability and texture sensitivity, but does not predict component lifetime or directly simulate observed failures.
narrate.key_results: The authors report that about 40 finite elements per grain were sufficient for converged in-grain stress distributions, and selected a 120-micrometer RVE containing about 615 grains; increasing the size to 160 micrometers produced little additional reduction in variability while taking about four times as long. The PCE surrogate was trained using 200 simulations, with 80 percent used for training and 20 percent for validation, and its predicted stress-strain curves showed close agreement with held-out simulations; the paper reports an orders-of-magnitude speedup over conventional Monte Carlo analysis but gives no numerical speedup or prediction-error metric. At yield strain, the reported mean stress was 393.36 megapascals, with bounds of 378.64 to 409.15 megapascals; at 1.0 percent strain, the mean was 444.77 megapascals, with bounds of 424.25 to 465.98 megapascals; at 3.0 percent strain, the mean was 500.61 megapascals, with bounds of 472.94 to 527.45 megapascals. Sensitivity analysis identified Cube and Goss texture components as the dominant influences on stress variability, while Brass, S1, S2, S3, Copper, and Taylor had minimal effects.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that CPFE calibration is numerically underdetermined and can have nonunique solutions. They also note that because calibration uses a noncyclic experiment, isotropic and kinematic hardening cannot be separated.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The surrogate is checked against simulated responses for a random holdout, not against independent measurements of degradation, fatigue life, or component failure. Its uncertainty inputs are texture fractions bounded from a particular welded specimen, so the predictions may not transfer to other weld procedures, materials, or service conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Extend the framework to cyclic loading and explicit fatigue or crack-growth models, and examine the effects of service conditions and other degradation mechanisms such as creep or environmental damage. Validate the predictions against independent tests and field data from multiple weldments, and assess how local texture-driven responses combine into component-level failure risk.

narrate.summary: Rare structural failures are difficult to estimate because they occur in low-probability regions and evaluating system performance can require costly simulations. The paper proposes Tail Stratified Sampling (TSS), which partitions the input distribution into strata that progressively reach farther into its tails and allocates samples across those strata. Its estimator uses the probability of each stratum and observed failures, and can omit a region known to be safe. The authors evaluate it using analytical reliability benchmarks and simulated structural models, including beam, oscillator, buckling, and cable examples. TSS is effective when its safe region isolates the failure-relevant tails, but its performance can degrade in high dimensions when that region is poorly chosen.
narrate.key_results: Across seven two-dimensional analytical problems with failure probabilities from about 10 to the minus 2 to 10 to the minus 9, TSS had at least one order of magnitude lower coefficient of variation than Subset Simulation in the reported comparisons; Subset Simulation did not converge for the Black Swan case. With 1,000 total samples, TSS achieved about 10 percent coefficient of variation across those examples, while Subset Simulation struggled to reach that level even with 10,000 or more samples. In the seven-dimensional stable buckling case, TSS estimates had coefficients of variation about two times lower than Subset Simulation across sample sizes. In high-dimensional examples, TSS performed worse than Subset Simulation when the design-point safe region failed to isolate relevant tails, but the cable example’s physically defined safe region produced less than 10 percent coefficient of variation at small sample sizes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method depends on identifying a useful safe region and meaningful tail strata, which can be difficult in high dimensions. It does not guide samples toward the failure region within each stratum, and conditional failure probabilities cannot be controlled by construction. A poorly chosen safe region can therefore make estimation inefficient.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses analytical examples and simulated structural models; it does not validate the reported performance against field observations. The variance expressions assume independent samples within strata, while the general discussion allows Markov chain sampling, whose dependence may affect those variance calculations; the paper does not provide a wall-clock cost comparison across methods.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose methods to identify lower-dimensional transformations or subspaces that make tail definition more effective, including data-driven and surrogate-based approaches. They also suggest combining TSS with importance sampling or other methods that guide sampling toward failure regions within tail strata, and using auxiliary system outputs correlated with performance.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on field data and on infrastructure models with changing operating conditions and multiple interacting failure mechanisms. Further work could also assess uncertainty in estimated stratum boundaries and safe-region definitions, and connect failure-probability estimates to system-level risk and engineering decisions.

narrate.summary: This paper addresses residual-lifetime prediction when units degrade at different rates, making a single homogeneous population assumption unsuitable. It models each unit’s degradation with a linear path and allows the distribution of unit-specific slopes to be flexible through a normal-mixture model with a Dirichlet process prior. Posterior parameter draws are used to approximate each unit’s residual-lifetime distribution, with Gibbs sampling and a transformation-based simulation method used for computation. The method is evaluated in simulated settings and on fatigue-crack measurements from 21 units, where failure is defined by crossing a crack-size threshold. The proposed method often helps represent slower-degrading subgroups, but overall prediction accuracy is usually similar to the parametric comparator and predicted median lifetimes are often too high.
narrate.key_results: In the fatigue-crack analysis, using the positive-lifetime version of the proposed model with the second prior setting gave a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.046 and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.209; the parametric comparator gave 0.046 and 0.212, respectively. In a simulated three-component Weibull-slope case with 10 units and 11 observations per unit, the positive-lifetime semi-parametric model had RMSE 0.477 and MAE 0.572, compared with 2.258 and 1.306 for the parametric model. Across the simulated cases, the authors report that the methods’ errors are generally similar as sample size and observations per unit increase, with the semi-parametric approach often better for slower-degrading units and the parametric approach often better for the fastest-degrading units. In the fatigue-crack data, estimated medians were about 0.053 to 0.070 million cycles while the reported true residual lifetimes ranged from 0.001 to 0.050 million cycles; most reported predictive intervals contained the true values.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that predicted median residual lifetimes are higher than the true values in most cases, which they attribute to a long upper tail in the posterior-averaged distribution. They also report poor tail estimation when the simulated random-effect distributions are skewed, and note that the parametric method often performs better for the fastest-degrading units. For very slowly degrading units, both methods can produce wide predictive intervals and fail to predict distant failures precisely.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes a linear degradation path, independent normally distributed measurement errors, and positive degradation slopes; these assumptions may not fit nonlinear degradation, correlated sensor errors, or units with non-monotone behavior. narrate.summary: The paper studies how much hyperparameter tuning can improve a Random Survival Forest (RSF) used to predict time to failure for predictive maintenance. It measures gains both for tuning the whole model and for tuning one hyperparameter at a time, using the concordance index (C-index) and Brier score. The experiments use four subsets of a public benchmark dataset that simulates aircraft-engine degradation, with a five-fold cross-validation framework and an exhaustive search of 330,000 configurations per subset. Tuning improved both discrimination and calibration on all four subsets. The authors find that the most useful hyperparameters depend on the performance measure and dataset, so tuning choices matter.
narrate.key_results: Compared with default settings, the tuned models improved the C-index by an average of 0.0547, or about 7.5%, and reduced the Brier score by an average of 0.0199, or about 14.6%. Improvements in both measures were reported for each of the four subsets. The number of trees and the number of variables considered at each split had the highest average contribution to C-index gains; terminal-node size and the number of variables considered at each split had the strongest effects on Brier score. Split criterion had negative average tunability for the C-index and effects near zero with wide variation for the Brier score, indicating that its effect was inconsistent across datasets.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes the New Generalized Fisk distribution, an extension of the log-logistic lifetime distribution with four parameters. It addresses variation in failure times rather than modeling a physical degradation process. The authors derive distribution properties, including the density, cumulative distribution, survival, and hazard functions, and estimate parameters using maximum likelihood estimation. They assess estimation through simulations and apply the model to failure-time data for 101 participants. The authors report that the proposed model fits this data better than five competing distributions under the model-comparison measures they used.
narrate.key_results: The real-data analysis uses 101 failure times measured in hours. The proposed model has an Akaike information criterion of 210.65, compared with 213.25 for the next-lowest model, Kumaraswamy Weibull; its Bayesian information criterion is 221.54 versus 223.71, and its Cramer-von Mises statistic is 0.09 versus 0.15. The authors report that their simulation results show estimates becoming more consistent with the true parameter values as sample size increases; the simulations used 1,000 repetitions and sample sizes from 25 to 500. For example, in the first simulation case with sample size 500, the reported estimates were 1.5818 for alpha, 2.0045 for beta, 2.7440 for theta, and 0.1888 for delta, against generating values of 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 0.25.

narrate.summary: Traditional reserve-margin constraints do not directly capture forced outages, hourly renewable variability, or coincidence between low renewable output and peak demand, and can lead to excess capacity. The paper models reliability-feasible generation mixes with a weighted oblique decision tree (WODT) trained on simulated reliability assessments, then expresses those feasible regions as constraints for generation expansion planning (GEP). The reliability simulations use forced outage rates and 8,760-hour renewable and load data, and assess whether loss of load hours (LOLH) meet the stated threshold. The method is evaluated in a 20-year Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) planning case using operational time-series data and generated training samples. The reported results show that the reliability constraints meet the LOLH criterion while lowering total planning cost relative to the reserve-margin-based comparison method.
narrate.key_results: With reliability verification constraints (RVC-GEP), LOLH is at most 2.40 in every planning year; in year 1 it falls from 44.58 without the embedded constraints to 2.34. The authors report that the trained tree assigns more than 99.9% of samples to correctly labeled leaves. Compared with the reserve-margin method (RM-GEP), RVC-GEP reduces investment cost by USD 1.66 billion and increases operating cost by USD 0.95 billion, yielding a net cost saving of USD 0.71 billion. Capacity margins are also lower under RVC-GEP, including decreases of 0.0317, 0.0559, 0.0573, and 0.0479 in the final four planning years.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes reliability-based design optimization (RBDO) using a large language model (LLM) to generate candidate designs, with a Kriging surrogate and Monte Carlo simulation used to estimate reliability. In the vehicle case, the surrogate-based solution had cost 25.59, compared with 25.21 for the genetic algorithm and 24.14 for the first-order reliability method; the authors describe the language-model result as near-optimal. narrate.summary: Maximum likelihood estimates can be biased when some test units do not follow the assumed lifetime model. This paper models nondestructive one-shot device testing under progressive-stress accelerated life testing, assuming a log-logistic lifetime and a tampered failure rate model. It proposes exponential-polynomial divergence estimation, studies its large-sample behavior and influence function, and uses concrete score matching to select its tuning parameters. It also optimizes sample allocations and inspection times under budget and duration limits. Simulations and a laboratory miniature-light-bulb data set indicate that the robust estimator is less affected by contamination, while the best tuning-parameter selection method depends on the data and contamination level.
narrate.key_results: The simulation used 75 devices across three stress groups and 1,000 generated data sets, with contamination rates from 0 to 0.16. At contamination rates of 0.12 and 0.16, the tuning parameters selected by concrete score matching gave lower reported RMSE+ values than the existing selection methods in the comparison: 0.126283 at 0.12 and 0.338221 at 0.16, compared with the next-lowest values of 0.248003 and 0.397445, respectively. In the miniature-light-bulb analysis, the bootstrap goodness-of-fit test gave a statistic of 3.848737 and an approximate p-value of 0.756; the iterative Warwick and Jones method had the lowest reported bootstrap RMSE+, 0.001378, compared with 0.002379 for concrete score matching. For the illustrated optimal-design setting, the paper reports that the density-power-divergence estimator with tuning parameter gamma equal to 0.3 gave the best strategy; the reported cost was USD 8,150.890 and the trace of the estimated covariance matrix was 0.000071 under that design.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a scalable second-order reliability method (SORM) for estimating rare event probabilities in stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with multiplicative Brownian noise. A direct extension of the usual finite-dimensional determinant calculation fails to scale with time resolution and can give an incorrect prefactor. The authors instead derive a formula using a regularized Carleman–Fredholm determinant and a corrected trace, and implement its numerical evaluation using automatic differentiation in JAX. They test the approach on a predator–prey model and a two-dimensional random advection–diffusion model of pollutant transport, using simulated paths and computational model outputs. The corrected estimates agree well with Monte Carlo simulations in these examples while keeping the number of equation evaluations roughly stable as resolution increases.
narrate.key_results: For the predator–prey model at noise strength 0.01 and threshold 0.5, 520,000 Monte Carlo simulations gave a 95% confidence interval of 1.56 × 10⁻⁴ to 2.32 × 10⁻⁴, while the corrected estimate at the highest reported resolution was 1.85 × 10⁻⁴. Across thresholds, estimates using the corrected formula agreed well with simulations using 900 million samples for each of three noise strengths: 0.001, 0.004, and 0.01. In the pollutant example, the corrected estimates agreed well with simulations using approximately 500,000 samples at noise strength 0.05 and 1 million at 0.1; at a target concentration near 0.15, the reported prefactor values across three resolutions ranged from 0.490017 to 0.507641. The largest reported calculation used a spatial resolution of 256 by 256 and 2,048 time steps, processed a naively represented matrix with about 7 × 10¹⁶ entries without assembling it, and took approximately one hour on a single core; the authors report that 200 leading eigenvalues sufficed for the displayed determinant approximations.

key_equations.explanation: The rate function I(z) is half the squared path-space norm of eta_z, the noise realization minimizing half the squared norm subject to the noise-to-observable map F reaching threshold z.

key_equations.name: Rare-event probability estimate
key_equations.explanation: The probability P at noise strength epsilon of exceeding threshold z is approximated by the exponential rate I(z), multiplied by the prefactor C(z) and the displayed noise-strength and constant factors.

key_equations.name: Corrected prefactor for multiplicative noise
key_equations.explanation: Here P is projection onto noise perturbations orthogonal to eta_z, A is the scaled second derivative of the noise-to-observable map at the optimal noise, tilde A is the correction for the less regular part of that derivative, e is eta_z normalized to unit length, Id is the identity operator, det2 is the regularized determinant, and tr is the operator trace.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that although the approximation is asymptotically exact, it can be inaccurate for a complicated failure region and should not replace sampling methods in such cases. For simplicity, their theory assumes a unique, nondegenerate design point and a finite time horizon, excluding issues such as metastability and degeneracies. They also note that checking the theorem’s assumptions can be challenging and that its rigorous scope is SDEs in finite-dimensional state spaces, while its application to the illustrated stochastic partial differential equation is supported numerically.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical validation uses two constructed examples and simulated data, not field measurements or operational reliability data, so performance on real systems is not established. The pollutant example also relies on smooth, low-rank random forcing, and conclusions about scalability may not carry over to models with high-rank or rough forcing. The results depend on numerical optimization and truncated eigenvalue calculations, whose approximation errors are not given as comprehensive bounds.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the approach to more realistic advection–diffusion problems and extending it to rough differential equations and singular stochastic partial differential equations. They also identify rigorous error estimates for determinant and trace approximations as valuable future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation on field or operational data and comparison with established reliability analyses for real engineering systems. Further studies could include uncertain operating conditions and covariates, multiple interacting failure modes or system-level failure events, and decision-focused uses of the resulting probability estimates.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes the Bi-Failure Modes (BFM) model for systems with two competing causes of failure, combining a Dhillon lifetime distribution for one cause and an exponential-power distribution for the other. The model represents several failure-rate shapes, including bathtub and roller-coaster patterns, which some existing competing-risk models do not capture well. It uses a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)-based Bayesian framework to estimate model parameters and reliability quantities, with a likelihood that allows right-censored observations. The authors apply the method to two real test datasets: 58 high-voltage endurance-tested electrodes, including 13 still operating when the test ended, and electrical-appliance lifetime data. The BFM generally fits these datasets better than five compared models, although it misses the final increasing-rate portion of the appliance data.
narrate.key_results: For the electrode data, the BFM achieved the lowest values on six of seven reported fit measures among the six compared models; its negative log-likelihood was 274.79, and its Akaike information criterion was 557.59. Its Bayesian estimate of mean time to failure was 241.89, compared with 243.88 from maximum-likelihood estimation. For the appliance data, the BFM had the best values on all seven fit measures, with negative log-likelihood 53.693 and Akaike information criterion 115.39; Bayesian and maximum-likelihood mean time to failure estimates were 2220.42 and 2254.41. The estimated cause-specific failure shares under the Bayesian model were 69.8% and 30.2% for the electrode causes, compared with empirical shares of 60% and 40%; for the appliance causes they were 62.6% and 37.4%, compared with empirical shares of 51.5% and 48.5%.

key_equations.explanation: Here h(x) is the overall failure rate at time x, and nu, theta, tau, and zeta are the BFM scale and shape parameters defined in the survival equation.

key_equations.explanation: Here F_k(x) is the probability of failure from cause k by time x, h_k(t) is that cause's failure rate at time t, and S(t) is the system's probability of surviving beyond t.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the BFM does not correctly identify the final part of the appliance dataset's empirical roller-coaster failure rate, specifically its last increasing-rate segment. They also note that the model was developed mainly for non-monotone failure-rate data and has not yet been tested on monotone failure-rate data.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes independent failure processes, so it may not represent systems where one failure mechanism changes the risk of another. The evidence comes from only two small, existing test datasets, with no external field-data validation; its performance for other products, operating conditions, or larger systems is therefore uncertain.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating how the BFM can more accurately predict the final roller-coaster segment seen in the appliance data. They also propose testing the model on datasets with monotone failure rates.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the independence assumption with models that allow dependent causes and assess performance under changing loads, environments, and other relevant covariates. Prospective field validation and analysis of how cause-specific estimates inform system-level maintenance or design decisions would also help establish engineering value.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses uncertainty in aircraft-engine remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, where censoring can make ordinary regression predictions biased. It models survival probabilities using a Rashomon set: multiple survival models with performance close to the best model, rather than relying only on one selected model. The authors train 19 survival models on the four CMAPSS benchmark subsets, use an 80% training and 20% testing split, and examine censoring times of 200, 225, and 250 cycles. They find that the range of survival predictions across similarly performing models varies by subset and censoring time, supporting the use of model multiplicity to expose uncertainty.
narrate.key_results: The Rashomon sets contained 5 models for FD001, 4 for FD002, 4 for FD003, and 8 for FD004; their mean C-index values and standard deviations were 0.8259 ± 0.0204, 0.7189 ± 0.0124, 0.8707 ± 0.0181, and 0.8027 ± 0.0146, respectively. FD003 had the highest reported mean C-index, while FD002 had the lowest. At 250 cycles, the prediction range was below 5% for FD001, exceeded 15% for FD002, and was around 8% for FD004; the authors also report that uncertainty exceeded 12% for FD002 and FD003 at 225 cycles and 15% at 250 cycles. The paper does not report a comparison of prediction error or maintenance cost against a single-model baseline.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a gradient-free extension of the Approximate Sampling Target with Post-processing Adjustment (ASTPA) framework for estimating rare-event and failure probabilities. The method addresses the difficulty of finding rare failure regions in high-dimensional, nonlinear models when analytical gradients are unavailable. It constructs a smooth target that emphasizes failure regions, discovers candidate failure samples to initialize preconditioned Crank–Nicolson (pCN) chains, and estimates the target’s normalizing constant using inverse importance sampling (IIS). The authors evaluate the method on mathematical limit-state functions, a 34-story structure, and a steel plate model, using simulated inputs in Gaussian space. Across these examples, the method generally estimates probabilities accurately with fewer model evaluations and lower variability than the compared gradient-free methods.
narrate.key_results: Across 500 independent simulations per method, the proposed method’s estimates were close to the reference probabilities from standard Monte Carlo calculations. For the 34-story structure, the estimated failure probabilities were 2.44 × 10⁻⁵, 1.22 × 10⁻⁶, and 2.48 × 10⁻⁷ for the three displacement thresholds; corresponding coefficients of variation were 0.14, 0.22, and 0.27, with 7,540 model evaluations in each case. For the steel plate problem, the estimate was 1.01 × 10⁻⁶ with a coefficient of variation of 0.16 and 7,247 model evaluations, compared with 7,611 evaluations and a coefficient of variation of 0.21 for improved cross-entropy importance sampling. In the 200-dimensional decic examples, the proposed method’s coefficients of variation ranged from 0.26 to 0.34, with 25,434 to 35,072 model evaluations; it used fewer evaluations and had lower variability than the reported sequential importance sampling and adaptive conditional sampling subset simulation results.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that this gradient-free method is designed for Gaussian spaces and that direct application in non-Gaussian spaces remains future work. They also state that the parameters used in the numerical examples were carefully chosen but not optimized.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing gradient-free variants for direct estimation in non-Gaussian spaces. They also propose extending the framework to high-dimensional first-passage problems under various settings.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method to predict how long an injection molding machine will run before failure, using the sequence of running without an alert, running with an alert, and failure. It models the two running-state durations with exponential distributions and the number of events before failure with a shifted Poisson distribution, then relates model parameters to selected sensor readings. The data comprise six days of operational records from one machine: 45 epochs, 3,190 running events, 45 failures, and readings from 72 sensors. The authors use random forests to screen sensors and regression models to connect selected sensors to event rates and counts. On these data, predicted failure times agree more closely with observed times than predictions from a Cox proportional hazards model.
narrate.key_results: For the 45 epochs, the proposed model had a mean squared error of 1,299,394.36, mean absolute error of 796.38, maximum error of 2,881.12, and correlation of 0.89 between predicted and observed failure times. The corresponding Cox proportional hazards results were 5,389,542.03, 1,102.77, 10,477.12, and 0.48; thus, its mean squared error was more than four times that of the proposed model. The base-model rate estimates were 0.0261 for running without an alert and 0.0738 for running with an alert, and the estimated probability that an epoch starts without an alert was 0.7778. In sensor classification tests, the running-versus-failure random forest had 95.85% testing accuracy, while the three-state classifier had 52.61% testing accuracy.

narrate.summary: Rare failures in sequential autonomous systems can be difficult to estimate with ordinary simulation because failures may require many costly runs to observe. The proposal is trained using samples from a smoothed approximation of the failure-trajectory distribution, and the final probability estimate corrects for the change in sampling distribution. The method is evaluated in simulated inverted-pendulum, pedestrian-crosswalk, aircraft-collision-avoidance, and F-16 ground-collision-avoidance systems. It produces more accurate failure-probability estimates than the tested Monte Carlo and importance-sampling baselines in all four problems.
narrate.key_results: The reference failure probabilities were estimated using 10 million Monte Carlo samples, and each reported method metric was averaged over 10 trials of 50,000 samples each. The proposed method's signed relative errors were -0.04 ± 0.06 for the pendulum, -0.02 ± 0.13 for the crosswalk, -0.05 ± 0.27 for aircraft collision avoidance, and 0.06 ± 0.10 for the F-16 system. Its absolute relative errors were 0.06 ± 0.03, 0.09 ± 0.09, 0.18 ± 0.21, and 0.09 ± 0.07, respectively; the best competing baseline for those problems reported 0.47 ± 0.16, 0.22 ± 0.11, 0.26 ± 0.43, and 0.94 ± 0.58. narrate.summary: Robotic manipulators can lose end-effector position accuracy, and heavier-payload tasks can accelerate this degradation. The paper models accuracy degradation as Brownian motion with a random drift that depends linearly on task severity, while a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) represents changes in task severity. It estimates the model parameters from periodic accuracy inspections and task histories, then calculates the remaining useful life (RUL) distribution using either an effective-rate approximation or Monte Carlo simulation. The framework is evaluated on simulated planar and spatial robot fleets, with 25 robots in each fleet and tasks involving 1 kg and 5 kg payloads. Both methods predict shorter lifetimes when future schedules contain a larger share of higher-severity tasks.
narrate.key_results: For the planar fleet, mean prediction errors for the effective-rate method and simulation method were, respectively, 40.5% and 46.3% at 30% of true lifetime, and 2.9% and 3.6% at 90%. For the spatial fleet, the corresponding errors were 33.2% and 24.4% at 30%, and 3.3% and 6.4% at 90%. The fixed-degradation-rate baseline had much larger planar errors, including 228.5% at 30% and 14.3% at 90%; the deterministic-task baseline performed comparably in most cases but assumes advance knowledge of future tasks. Total computation time for all 25 robots was 5.49 seconds for the planar effective-rate method and 11,080.37 seconds for its simulation counterpart; for the spatial fleet, the times were 5.09 and 9,218.62 seconds. The authors’ theoretical result establishes a conservative lower-bound relationship for expected lifetime under long prediction horizons, rather than an unconditional equality between the approaches.

For loss of ship steering ability, the estimated top-event probability is 5.4E-02, slightly above the cited study’s 4.86E-02. The best protocol-parameter-only model had median and maximum MAPE of 11.06% and 11.35%, respectively. The designed model's median RMSE was 97.33, compared with 86.17 for the automated-feature model and 107.10 for the protocol-parameter-only model.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a robust Bayesian method for estimating the lifetimes of nondestructive one-shot devices tested under step-stress accelerated life testing (SSALT). It uses a cumulative risk model (CRM), which allows a lag before a stress change affects the hazard and avoids an abrupt change in the hazard at the stress transition. The method replaces the ordinary likelihood contribution with a density power divergence (DPD)-based objective, considers several prior choices, and uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for computation. The authors evaluate it with simulated Weibull and Gompertz data and a laboratory light-bulb test dataset. Their main finding is that the robust Bayesian estimates are less affected by the simulated contamination than conventional likelihood-based estimates, while Bayesian estimates generally perform well on uncontaminated data.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 50 units and 1,000 generated datasets, robust Bayesian estimates generally had smaller bias and root mean square error (RMSE) than conventional Bayesian estimates under contamination; for Weibull data, the order-restricted robust estimates with tuning value 0.3 had RMSEs of 0.005402, 0.005540, 0.005352, 0.005352, and 0.005519 across the five parameters. In the light-bulb analysis, the experiment included 64 bulbs, with 11 surviving to the 140-hour stopping time; the estimated lag was 0.001. Bootstrap goodness-of-fit tests gave p-values of 0.660 for the Weibull model and 0.836 for the Gompertz model. For the bulb data, reported Weibull bootstrap RMSEs for the conventional maximum likelihood estimates were 0.004828, 0.006648, 0.019801, and 0.016239, compared with 0.001122, 0.001140, 0.001148, and 0.001155 for order-restricted robust Bayesian estimates at tuning value 0.2. The reported robust Bayes factors favored the tested null hypotheses: values ranged from 31.445540 to 88.698669 for Weibull and from 14.312101 to 26.448023 for Gompertz, with the paper’s interpretation varying from positive to strong support.

The fixed 130°C threshold had nearly perfect detection results, including recall of 1.000, but its median detection time was 98 minutes and median time remaining before failure was 15 minutes. narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of finding minimal cut sets when the number of possible component-failure configurations grows exponentially with system size. It then uses quantum amplitude amplification to increase the chance of sampling configurations that are minimal cut sets. The evaluation uses theoretical comparisons and numerical experiments on a quantum simulator, including a simulated fault tree with eight basic events and 16 minimal cut sets. In that example, the proposed method substantially reduced the expected number of samples needed to find all minimal cut sets compared with Monte Carlo sampling and a simpler quantum approach.
narrate.key_results: For the example with eight basic events, the initial probability of sampling a minimal cut set was 0.0625. narrate.summary: Expensive evaluations of an engineering performance function can make reliability analysis impractical, while simpler approximations may be inaccurate for nonlinear behavior near the failure boundary. In 100 repeated simulations, the uncorrelated proposed rule produced the same results as the U learning rule. narrate.summary: The paper examines how dependence between component failure times changes the reliability of redundant systems. It develops three models: a linear dependence model, a model in which all components can fail together, and a model in which some components can fail together. The authors use simulated failure times, based on identical Weibull distributions with shape parameter one, to study three-component parallel, voting, and series architectures. In the marginal common-cause model, the mean time to failure changes nonlinearly with the dependence parameter for all three architectures. The study reports an average of 10^7 simulations for each model, architecture, and parameter value, amounting to 1.8 billion random-variable draws; it reports no field-data comparison or single overall accuracy score.

narrate.summary: The paper models systems exposed to random shocks that cause damage, continuous aging that lowers the failure threshold, and self-healing that reduces shock damage. narrate.summary: The paper develops robust estimation and hypothesis-testing methods for step-stress accelerated life tests when failures are observed only at scheduled inspections. It models lifetimes with a Weibull distribution, assumes the scale changes log-linearly with stress, and represents inspection-interval failure counts as multinomial data. The proposed restricted estimators use density power divergence and can enforce parameter constraints; the paper also constructs a robust Rao-type test from these estimators. The methods are assessed theoretically and in simulations based on a solar-lighting-device experiment, with deliberately contaminated interval counts. The main finding is that the maximum-likelihood approach and low-robustness settings can degrade substantially under contamination, while moderate or larger tuning values reduce that degradation.
narrate.key_results: The simulation used 200 devices, 14 inspection times, and 10,000 repetitions, with contamination applied to interval-failure probabilities. Under heavy contamination, the classical and low-tuning Rao-type tests had empirical rejection levels as high as about 0.3 when the nominal level was 0.05. Tests using moderate or larger tuning values retained more acceptable levels, and the authors identify values above 0.4 as a possible compromise between robustness and efficiency. The reported plots show lower parameter and mean-time-to-failure estimation error for robust settings under contamination, but the paper does not give exact numerical error values in the text.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of monitoring degradation when detailed health labels are costly or unavailable. On the milling data, the resulting index tracks measured wear without using those measurements in model training. For the spray-coating data, the method detects the expert-indicated end-of-life period for all four pairs, although no ground-truth health-index trajectory is available for that application.
narrate.key_results: On the milling benchmark, the best reported approach, real-time diversity DeepSAD with APAIC feature fusion, achieved an average adjusted RMSE of 14.04 with a standard deviation of 0.73 and an average correlation of 0.967 with ground truth. Its error was close to the 12.70 reported for a supervised stacked sparse autoencoder trained using ground-truth labels. On the spray-coating data, the diversity-enhanced approach detected end of life for all four nozzle-electrode pairs and had an average alarm delay of 1.379 hours, compared with 3.632 hours for real-time APAIC DeepSAD and 7.784 hours for DeepSAD; the latter two methods missed alarms on some pairs. narrate.summary: Markovian degradation models can give biased reliability estimates when degradation increments depend on the history of the process, and ignoring differences between units can also distort estimates. This paper models degradation with fractional Brownian motion to represent memory and a random unit-specific degradation rate to represent unit-to-unit variability, while also accounting for external stress. The authors develop an expectation-maximization method to estimate the model parameters and use simulation to estimate lifetime and reliability. They evaluate the approach using simulated accelerated degradation data and temperature-stressed tuner degradation measurements. The proposed model and estimator perform better than the compared methods in the reported simulation and tuner analyses.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation study, the true Hurst exponent was 0.1 and the proposed estimator gave 0.117, with a reported 90% confidence interval of 0.012 to 0.181. Across the nine sample-size and measurement combinations, the proposed method's total relative error ranged from 0.044 to 0.235; the two-step maximum-likelihood method had errors from 0.624 to 1.802, and its Hurst-exponent bias was nearly 100% with few measurements and around 40% with more measurements, compared with less than 5% for the proposed method. In the simulated model comparison, the full model had the best reported Akaike information criterion, -1611.65, compared with -1200.96, -920.15, and -853.79 for the three reduced models, and its normal-condition reliability estimate was closest to the simulated truth. In the tuner case, the full model had a deterministic-trend error index of 0.1335, compared with 0.1490, 0.1429, and 0.1849 for the alternatives, and was generally better at predicting degradation boundaries and extrapolating to omitted stress levels. For the tuner at its normal use temperature of 20°C, the reported lower boundary of reliability at 6,000 hours was nearly 0.99 at the 90% confidence level.

narrate.summary: This review considers why disk failure classifiers can miss faulty disks when failure examples are rare compared with healthy-disk examples. It organizes approaches into data-level methods that alter the training data, algorithm-level methods that change classifier learning, and hybrid methods that combine these strategies. The discussion draws on the Backblaze disk dataset and on previously published studies using disk health measurements, including Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology (SMART) data. It describes sampling, synthetic data generation, cost-sensitive learning, transfer learning, and classifier ensembles, together with their reported strengths and drawbacks. The paper is a survey and does not present a new predictive model or an original comparative experiment.
narrate.key_results: The review gives no pooled performance estimate or head-to-head evaluation of the approaches it covers. It notes that when the class ratio exceeds 20 to 1, a classifier can reach 90 percent accuracy while still performing poorly on the rare class. A cited disk study reduced the positive-to-negative sample ratio to 1 to 10 using undersampling, and another cited study reported a failure detection rate (FDR) of 96 percent and a false alarm rate (FAR) of 0.5 percent. The review also describes conditional table generative adversarial network (CTGAN) and integrated generative adversarial network (GAN) approaches as promising for balancing disk data, but provides no comparable numerical results for them.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that data-level preprocessing may be poorly suited to datasets with very high imbalance, and that selecting an effective oversampling rate is difficult. They also identify the risk of losing useful information through undersampling, the difficulty of estimating true misclassification costs, and the challenge of preserving the data distribution while reducing imbalance.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review does not describe a systematic search or study-selection process, so readers cannot assess how comprehensively the cited literature was identified. It also does not evaluate the surveyed methods on a common dataset and metric set, making the reported results difficult to compare directly.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify transfer learning as a promising way to address disk types with few failure examples. They also propose evolutionary learning and integrated machine-learning models as research directions, and call for better selection of sampling rates using information about the data distribution.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could compare the surveyed approaches using consistent time-based splits and disk-level evaluation, then validate the strongest methods on operational data from additional storage environments. It could also connect missed-failure and false-alarm performance to maintenance decisions and costs, and examine how operating conditions and disk types affect generalization.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses inefficient identification of pass-fail boundaries in expensive computer simulations, where entropy-only sampling can cluster runs near one part of a boundary and miss other parts. It combines a deep Gaussian process surrogate with triangulation-based candidate points and selects candidates from the Pareto set of predictive entropy and uncertainty. The authors evaluate the method on synthetic functions and a simulated RAE-2822 airfoil, using lift-to-drag ratio below 3 as the failure condition. For the airfoil, the seven inputs include flight conditions and airfoil shape parameters. The sequential method achieves better failure classification than the static designs it compares against, using substantially fewer airfoil simulation runs to exceed their performance.
narrate.key_results: On the airfoil simulation, the proposed sequential design outperformed static designs in sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score with as few as 200 simulator evaluations; the 500-run static Latin hypercube design required nearly 12 additional hours of computation. At 500 evaluations, the paper reports that the Bayesian deep Gaussian process also had better prediction accuracy and uncertainty scoring than the stationary Gaussian process and the variational deep Gaussian process on a 4,500-point holdout design. In synthetic tests on two- and five-dimensional plateau functions and a cross-in-tray function, the deep Gaussian process with Pareto-triangulation sampling generally achieved higher sensitivity than the compared sequential and static alternatives. The paper reports no single numerical summary score for these comparisons in its text.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that Delaunay triangulation can become prohibitively costly in higher dimensions; in their experience, eight dimensions approaches the tractability limit of the library they used unless the design is small. They also note that a deep Gaussian process may overfit stationary responses, and that exploration-oriented Pareto-triangulation sampling may underperform simpler approaches when the failure region or contour is simple. The authors identify batch acquisition and improved high-dimensional candidate generation as areas needing further study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on synthetic functions and a computational airfoil model, with no validation against field measurements or observed aircraft failures. The reported airfoil evaluation uses a holdout space-filling design and classification metrics, rather than directly demonstrating calibrated failure-probability estimates under a real operating-input distribution. The method also relies on posterior predictive summaries from sampled models, so its results may depend on sampling adequacy and surrogate assumptions that are not independently tested in the application.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing alternatives to Delaunay triangulation that retain its candidate-placement behavior in higher dimensions. They also suggest studying batch acquisition and incorporating the input probability distribution into sequential design so that learning can be prioritized in relevant regions of the failure contour.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method against field or experimental aerospace data and assess calibration of estimated failure probabilities across realistic operating distributions. It could also extend the approach to multiple failure mechanisms and system-level reliability, and quantify how decisions based on the learned contour affect engineering risk.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a way to estimate the remaining useful life (RUL) of software as its performance changes across releases, rather than over calendar time. narrate.key_results: The reported correlation between the CPV and response time was 0.95. The adjusted R squared values were 0.9798 for cluster A and 0.8796 for cluster B, with reported p-values of 0.00009 and 0.00036, respectively. The 2-fold cross-validation average score was 0.9629. In the test-data comparison, the actual and predicted response times were 5416 and 5248 milliseconds for release 5.0.2, and 5579 and 5634 milliseconds for release 5.0.3; among the four forecast release plans, Combo-1 had the longest predicted performance cycle before the 9-second threshold.

narrate.summary: This thesis examines deep learning for equipment health diagnosis and remaining useful life prediction, motivated by the need to reduce unplanned downtime and maintenance costs. It models equipment condition from sensor measurements, using neural networks for simulated turbofan engines and laboratory bearing vibration data. The data include a turbofan simulation benchmark, artificially faulted bearing tests from Case Western Reserve University, and accelerated bearing run-to-failure experiments from the FEMTO dataset. The thesis finds that recurrent networks produce less noisy turbofan life predictions than a feed-forward network, while convolutional networks classify bearing faults and health states with high reported test performance. It also proposes, but does not test, a vibration-monitoring approach for oilfield top drives.
narrate.key_results: For turbofan health classification, the reported test accuracy is 93.43%, with a receiver operating characteristic area of 0.9332. The long short-term memory model’s test mean absolute error for remaining useful life is 23.27 cycles; the author reports that its predictions are less noisy than those from the feed-forward model, but does not provide a directly comparable numerical error for that model. For the Case Western Reserve University bearing fault-type classifier, test accuracy is 98.71%. For the FEMTO healthy-versus-faulty bearing classifier, the paper reports test precision of 98.44%, recall of 0.9694, an F1 score of 0.9794, and a receiver operating characteristic area of 0.8348.

key_equations.name: Remaining useful life

narrate.limitations_stated: The author says that the proposed polynomial remaining-life labels cannot be claimed to represent real-world degradation, though they may help a learning algorithm capture trends in the data. Petroleum-field data were unavailable because of commercial and technical sensitivity, so the oilfield application is not validated on field data. The author also notes that the long short-term memory network has many more parameters and takes much longer to train than the feed-forward network.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The turbofan findings rely on simulated engines, and the bearing experiments use laboratory or accelerated test conditions; performance on operating oilfield equipment is therefore unknown. The FEMTO health classifier uses bearings from the first operating condition, so generalization across the other conditions is not established by that experiment. The paper does not clearly establish that all train, validation, and test splits separate individual machines or bearings, leaving possible dependence between samples as a concern.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author proposes applying the methods to oilfield equipment, particularly top drives, by making better use of existing sensor histories and adding vibration sensors. The proposed sensors would monitor bearings and gears in vertical, horizontal, and axial directions, with neural networks used to detect degradation or classify degradation patterns when sufficient historical data are available.

In the rare stochastic test, it found failures in about 9% of evaluations, compared with 0.041% for nominal sampling, whose estimated failure probability was 4.1 × 10⁻⁴. For the runway detector, it found 571 failures in 999 evaluations and estimated a failure probability of 5.8 × 10⁻³; the paper notes that ordinary Monte Carlo sampling was expected to find only about six failures in that budget.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to estimate probabilities for several structural events when high-fidelity simulations are costly and a surrogate trained for one event may perform poorly for another. narrate.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting remaining useful life (RUL) when there are few labelled examples of fatigue failure. It models fatigue crack growth in simulated aluminum alloy panels and uses strain measurements from three sensor positions. The method first trains recurrent neural networks on unlabelled, incomplete sensor sequences using either an autoencoder reconstruction task or an autoregressive forecasting task, then uses the learned representations to predict RUL from a small labelled dataset. Across experiments with different quantities of unlabelled and labelled data, pre-training often improves predictions when labelled data are scarce, with autoregressive pre-training generally outperforming the autoencoder approach. The study uses simulated data and reports lower fine-tuning time when pre-trained layers are frozen.
narrate.key_results: With 10,000 unlabelled structures and 10 labelled structures, the autoencoder approach reported a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of about 11–12%, compared with about 23% for its non-pre-trained counterpart. For the autoregressive model with sequences truncated at 60% of lifetime and 10 labelled structures, the MAPE was 7.34%, compared with 21.10% for the non-pre-trained autoregressive model. In one multi-step forecasting case, using 5 labelled structures and sequences truncated at 90% of lifetime, the MAPE was 13.24% with a 30-step horizon, versus 22.69% for the one-step autoregressive model. Freezing pre-trained layers reduced fine-tuning time by 1.5 to 2 times compared with the other tested models, although pre-training was not consistently beneficial and the non-pre-trained autoregressive model had lower error in some settings with 100 labelled structures.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a data-driven method for estimating reliability in parallel load-sharing systems, where component failure increases the hazard faced by surviving components. It approximates each stage's cumulative hazard function with piecewise linear segments, using likelihood-based estimation and allowing the hazard to increase after failures. The authors derive estimates for system reliability at a mission time, lifetime quantiles, mean time to failure, and mean residual time. They evaluate the method with simulations and data from 18 two-motor systems. In that example, the method fits better by the reported information criterion than two previously considered models, and the authors report estimates of system lifetime and mission reliability.
narrate.key_results: For the 18-system two-motor data, the piecewise linear approximation (PLA) model had an Akaike information criterion (AIC) of 369.34, compared with 409.65 for the best model of Franco and colleagues and 480.50 for the Weibull model of Asha and colleagues. A goodness-of-fit test gave a statistic of 0.414 and a Monte Carlo p-value of 0.71; the estimated load multiplier was 4.2712. The estimated mean time to failure (MTTF) was 221.36 days; estimated reliability at a mission time (RMT) fell from 0.963 at 102 days to 0.044 at 350 days, while estimated mean residual time (MRT) fell from 124.223 to 36.919 days at those same mission times. In simulations with 5,000 replications and sample sizes of 100 and 200, average parameter estimates were close to their generating values, but reported coverage for 95% confidence intervals varied from 68.70% to 99.94% across parameters and interval methods; simulations from Weibull and quadratic-hazard models also showed reasonably small absolute integrated errors (AIE).
