narrate.summary: A single remaining useful life estimate does not show how uncertain that estimate is, which can make it difficult to use in maintenance decisions. The paper applies conformal prediction to turn point estimates into intervals intended to contain the true remaining useful life at a chosen coverage level. It compares several interval methods, including methods designed to adapt interval widths and to account for non-exchangeable data. The evaluation uses sensor and operating-condition data from four simulated turbofan-engine datasets in the Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation benchmark. The authors find that non-exchangeable methods generally provide higher average coverage, while conformalized quantile regression generally produces narrower intervals.
narrate.key_results: Experiments used four benchmark datasets and were repeated over 15 random training-calibration splits, with 10% of training data reserved for calibration. The evaluated miscoverage rates were 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, and 0.25. Across the comparisons, non-exchangeable methods generally had higher average coverage, while conformalized quantile regression had the narrowest average intervals. Using a normalized nonconformity score often improved results, especially for datasets with changing operating conditions; the paper does not report exact numerical accuracy or interval-width results in its text.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Model-Agnostic Reliability Analysis (MAntRA) for estimating time-dependent failure probability when a system’s governing physics is unknown. It learns a stochastic differential equation (SDE) from measured system responses, then simulates that learned model and counts threshold exceedances to estimate failure probability. The equation discovery method uses Bayesian sparse selection and a variational approximation to represent uncertainty from noisy and limited measurements. The authors evaluate the approach on simulated data for three structural dynamics examples: a Duffing oscillator, a nonlinear three-degree-of-freedom oscillator, and a structure with a tuned mass damper. The discovered models produce failure-probability curves that closely track those from the known simulated systems, including predictions out to 30 seconds after training on one second of data.
narrate.key_results: For each example, the authors generated 500 noisy trajectories over one second, with 5% noise and a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz. In the single-degree-of-freedom Duffing example, estimated mass-normalized stiffness was 999.87 versus 1000, the diffusion parameter was 1.09 versus 1.00, and the nonlinear coefficient was 100369.79 versus 100000. In the three-degree-of-freedom example, estimated stiffnesses were 1000.00, 1999.67, and 2999.87 versus 1000, 2000, and 3000; failure probabilities closely matched the reference through 30 seconds. In the tuned-mass-damper example, most estimated damping and stiffness values were near their targets, but the sixth stiffness estimate was 873.39 versus 300; the estimated failure curve was broadly similar to the reference, and the paper reports good results through 30 seconds. The paper gives no numerical error metric for the failure-probability curves or runtime comparison.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of updating remaining useful life (RUL) predictions efficiently when degradation measurements arrive over time. It models monotone degradation with a gamma process and derives a conjugate Bayesian prior, first for similar systems and then for systems with different degradation rates. Three posterior-sampling methods are developed, and the prior parameters can be updated recursively as new measurements arrive. The methods are assessed using simulated data, laboratory measurements from laser devices, and train-wheel wear data. The authors report fast computation and reasonably accurate RUL predictions in both real-data examples.
narrate.key_results: Across 10,000 simulated datasets, the reported absolute relative errors for estimates of the model parameters and reliability at 4,500 hours were around 2%, while the error for mean time to failure was around 0.1%; the three sampling methods performed similarly. For one dataset, average computation time was 0.602 seconds for Gibbs sampling, 0.00341 seconds for discrete grid sampling (DGS), and 0.00499 seconds for sampling importance resampling (SIR), making the latter two more than one hundred times faster than Gibbs sampling. In the heterogeneous model, sampling time increased from 0.00328 to 0.00895 seconds for DGS and from 0.00448 to 0.0101 seconds for SIR as the number of systems increased from 2 to 50. In the laser and train-wheel examples, the authors report that RUL point predictions were close to the observed reference RULs; the reported 95% intervals covered the reference values at nearly all laser prediction times and all train-wheel measurement points.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the time-consuming, manually documented process of planning semiconductor failure analyses. It models generation of ordered failure analysis triplets (FATs) from a failure description (FDR) as a text-generation task, fine-tuning and comparing pre-trained language models. The main data set contains 5,809 successful semiconductor failure-analysis records from 2019, with ten description features and the associated analysis steps. The authors also introduce Levenshtein Sequential Evaluation (LESE), which evaluates ordered structured triplets using sequence edits. Fine-tuned Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) performs best overall among the compared models, but long sequences and exact equipment selection remain difficult.
narrate.key_results: On the reported model comparison, GPT-2 Large scored 22.46 on BLEU-1 and 17.60 on BLEU-3, and had ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L scores of 29.82 and 27.93, respectively; these results were better overall than the miniature GPT baseline, BART, and GPT-3. GPT-2 Medium achieved a perfect 100 percent LESE-1 and LESE-3 score on one example containing four expert triplets, but other short-sequence examples were substantially less accurate. For a seven-triplet example, the best reported LESE-1 result was 31.11 percent, and the models did not reproduce the expert’s exact equipment. In the authors’ equipment-order test, switching the equipment in two triplets changed LESE-3 from 100 percent to 50 percent, while BLEU-1 remained 100 percent, illustrating the proposed metric’s sensitivity to sequence differences.

narrate.summary: Crude Monte Carlo sampling becomes inefficient when structural failure is very rare, because it may require a very large number of samples to observe failures. The paper adapts the accelerated weight histogram (AWH) method to estimate these probabilities by guiding a Markov chain back and forth across threshold levels and adapting the sampling weights. It tests the method on a standard normal model with a known failure probability and on a simulated fiber bundle model with random fiber strengths. These are computational examples rather than measurements from operating structures. The method performs comparably to subset simulation on the normal example and gives more accurate estimates than the tested subset simulations on the fiber bundle example at comparable computational effort.
narrate.key_results: For the normal example, the estimated failure probability after 100,000 evaluations was 1.25 × 10^-9; across 50 runs, its relative root-mean-square (RMS) error was 0.2, compared with 0.17 for subset simulation at the same number of evaluations. At load 220, with 500,000 evaluations per run, the RMS relative error was about 0.25 for AWH and about 1.0 for subset simulation. The authors report that subset simulation could reproduce the AWH results in the load-200 example when its Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) updates were increased, but this required over 1.2 million function evaluations rather than the 200,000 used for AWH.

narrate.summary: The paper studies estimation and inspection planning when two dependent failure causes are monitored at scheduled times rather than observed at exact failure times. It models the competing lifetimes with the Marshall–Olkin bivariate exponential distribution and develops a robust minimum density power divergence estimator alongside the maximum likelihood estimator. It also develops a robust Wald test for whether the two cause-specific rates are equal and optimizes inspection times to balance experiment cost against estimator precision. The authors evaluate the methods using simulated interval failure counts and a real bivariate data set of 30 observations from an earlier study. Their simulations show that maximum likelihood estimates are more affected by contamination, while the robust estimates remain much less affected.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation, contaminated maximum likelihood bias for the first parameter set reached about -0.0195 for the shared-shock rate, compared with about -0.00056 on pure data; the robust estimator with tuning parameter 0.4 had contaminated bias about -0.00012 for that rate. The inspection-time optimization produced 4 Pareto solutions in the initial population and 42 after 100 generations. For the real-data fit, the approximate bootstrap p-values ranged from 0.2084 to 0.2235 across the reported estimators and tuning settings.

narrate.summary: Subset Simulation can produce unreliable failure-probability estimates when its Markov chains fail to explore important parts of a failure region, especially when that region has separated or difficult-to-reach modes. The paper proposes Niching Subset Simulation (NSuS), which partitions the input space and runs sampling branches in the separate regions; its hill valley graph (HVG) uses community detection and a support vector classifier to construct those partitions. The method estimates failure probabilities and can also identify separate failure modes and their contributions. It is tested on simulated piecewise-linear and mixture-of-normal examples, including a 100-dimensional case, and on two simulated oscillator reliability problems. Across these examples, NSuS usually reduces missed failure modes and often improves estimator variability compared with ordinary Subset Simulation, though the gains depend on the problem and come with partitioning overhead.
narrate.key_results: In 100 runs on the two-dimensional piecewise-linear example, NSuS produced non-degenerate runs in 98% of cases versus 35% for SuS; the joint estimator’s coefficient of variation was 1.10 versus 2.61, and mean performance-function evaluations were 4,934 plus 4 for partition construction versus 5,280. On the 100-dimensional version, the non-degenerate proportions were 95% versus 60%, while the joint coefficients of variation were 1.10 versus 1.34. For the mixture-of-normal example, NSuS was non-degenerate in 99% of runs versus 73%, with joint coefficients of variation of 0.77 versus 1.28; degenerate SuS runs estimated zero failure probability. For the two-degree-of-freedom mass-spring example, NSuS was non-degenerate in 92% of runs versus 55%, and the joint coefficients of variation were 0.82 versus 1.54; on the symmetric single-degree-of-freedom oscillator, the non-degenerate proportions were 99% versus 76%, but the joint coefficients of variation were similar at 1.07 and 1.15.

narrate.limitations_stated: NSuS can only detect and fully explore a niche if the initial samples include points in it, so the authors note that counterexamples can still be constructed. The described implementation can add computational cost, particularly when only one niche exists, and requires choices such as graph size. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated benchmark functions and structural models, not field measurements, so performance on real infrastructure remains unverified. The graph test checks the midpoint when no relevant search-history samples are available, which can miss a valley, and the linear classifier may not capture complex partition boundaries. The statistical results also rely on simplifying assumptions, including uncorrelated chain samples for the indicator functions and fixed partitions and thresholds in the theoretical analysis.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose pairing NSuS with more exploratory Markov chain methods, changing how computational resources are allocated across niches, and using more complex valley tests. narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on field-informed structural reliability cases and compare its failure-mode findings against observed failures or validated high-fidelity models. Study how dependent and non-Gaussian inputs, changing operating conditions, and system-level interactions affect partitioning and probability estimates, and assess whether the identified modes lead to better engineering decisions.

The nominal 95% coverage was not achieved by any approximate method, though transformed intervals generally had better coverage, especially under contamination. For the solar-light data, estimated mean lifetime increased from 5.468 to 5.717 hundred hours as the tuning value increased from 0 to 1, while estimated reliability at 400 hours stayed close to 0.59. narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Angular Control Chart (ACC) to address the inability of existing reliability charts to monitor multiple failure-state transitions simultaneously. It represents each transition in a multi-state system (MSS) on its own state line and uses angles based on observed time-to-failure (TTF) and distribution quantiles to signal possible improvement or degradation. The authors derive chart limits for exponential, Weibull, lognormal, Fréchet, and gamma lifetime distributions, with a generalized design allowing different distributions across transitions. They illustrate the method using simulated failure times, not field data. The examples show that the chart can indicate changes in individual transitions and overall reliability, but also suggest that aggregating failures can reduce sensitivity.
narrate.key_results: The chart uses an acceptable false-alarm probability of 0.27% in its examples. In Example I, the first 25 simulated observations had 12 points above and 13 below the center line; across all 50 observations, the authors identify two improvement points for one transition and one possible degradation point for another. In Example II, which groups times until every two failures, the chart finds one out-of-control point for that transition rather than two in Example I, which the authors say could indicate reduced sensitivity. In Example III, 33 of 50 points were above the center line, which the authors interpret as an overall reliability improvement; these are demonstrations, not comparative accuracy or error-rate estimates.

narrate.summary: Rare dangerous events make ordinary simulation inefficient for assessing autonomous-vehicle safety, and conservative risk bounds can be too large to compare system designs meaningfully. The paper presents Deep importance sampling, which trains a neural network to approximate the dangerous-event region and uses numerical optimization to find likely failure regions for targeted sampling. The method is tested on simulated vehicle crashes in a cut-in and tailgate scenario and on traffic-sign misclassifications using images from the public German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark. Importance-sampling estimates are compared with ordinary Monte Carlo sampling and two conservative variants. The authors find that their method gives estimates close to the reference values while reducing the sample requirement, with efficiency improving as events become rarer.
narrate.key_results: For the simulated vehicle-safety example, the estimated crash probability was about 2 × 10⁻⁵; at the reported 20% relative-error target, Deep importance sampling required 178,832 samples versus 431,210 for ordinary Monte Carlo, an acceleration rate of 2.41. For traffic-sign classification at rarity parameter gamma = 5.0, the estimated misclassification rate was about 2 × 10⁻⁶, and Deep importance sampling required 418,983 samples versus 18,181,798 for ordinary Monte Carlo, an acceleration rate of 43.4; its reported degree of conservativeness was 1.02. The conservative methods had higher reported acceleration rates in that classification experiment, but their estimates were 14.26 and 9.54 times the target for Robust Deep IS and Iterative Robust Deep IS, respectively. The authors report an acceleration rate up to 659 at gamma = 8.0, although the ordinary Monte Carlo sample requirement at that setting was approximated rather than measured directly.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a framework for estimating the chance that an aircraft design will pass or fail a flight certification maneuver despite uncertainty in its aerodynamic data. The data include computational results from vortex-lattice and fluid-dynamics simulations, plus wind- and water-tunnel measurements for the Common Research Model and Generic T-tail Transport. The framework samples probabilistic aerodynamic and control databases and evaluates them in simulations of a roll-capability maneuver. Results show that lower-fidelity analyses can misrepresent control effectiveness, while combining fidelity levels can support earlier, uncertainty-informed design decisions.
narrate.key_results: For the modified maneuver and its control limits, the estimated roll-metric failure rates were 6.0% using vortex-lattice data, 15.1% using vortex-lattice plus computational fluid-dynamics data, 39.2% using those sources plus wind-tunnel data, and 30.8% using wind-tunnel data alone. There were no pitch-metric failures in these cases; yaw-metric failure rates were 1.6%, 37.1%, 0.0%, and 0.0%, respectively. With sparse wind-tunnel data, the roll failure rate was 55.2% for the single-fidelity case and 65.3% for the multi-fidelity case; the localized-high-fidelity case reached 96.4%, illustrating that localization did not reliably reproduce the fuller-data results. For a target 95% simulated success rate, the reported required maximum aileron deflections ranged from 15.33 degrees to 17.05 degrees across the four full-data cases; for 100% success, they ranged from 18.21 degrees to 22.61 degrees.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The certification demonstration uses one aircraft configuration and one maneuver, with altered control-surface limits introduced to produce failures; its failure estimates therefore do not directly establish real-world certification reliability for an unmodified aircraft. narrate.summary: Structural health monitoring can improve maintenance decisions, but its economic benefit is difficult to establish, especially when environmental changes affect vibration measurements and damage data are scarce. The examples show that monitoring can reduce expected costs, with the estimated benefit varying substantially by the decision scenario.
narrate.key_results: For observed extreme events, the estimated Value of structural health monitoring was EUR 1.11 × 10^5 compared with intermittent inspections alone. When shock damage could occur without being observed, the estimated benefit increased to EUR 1.42 × 10^5, because monitoring detected deterioration jumps that inspection-only management could miss. For near-real-time decisions after an extreme event, the estimate was EUR 1.34 × 10^6, mainly because monitoring could prevent unnecessary bridge closures with high daily costs. With an authority-imposed repair threshold, the estimated benefit was EUR 7.70 × 10^4; these estimates exclude the life-cycle cost of the monitoring system itself.

narrate.summary: This paper compares Bayesian methods for choosing accelerated life testing models when their posterior distributions are too complex for closed-form calculation. It examines a generalized Eyring-Weibull model and a generalized Eyring-Birnbaum-Saunders model, and compares the deviance information criterion with several ways of estimating Bayes factors. The models describe how temperature and humidity stresses affect device lifetimes, with gamma priors on the model parameters. The application uses 21 complete failure times from an accelerated test of a device at different temperature and humidity combinations. The main finding is that model-selection conclusions vary by estimation method, although the deviance information criterion and posterior predictive comparisons generally give stronger support to the Birnbaum-Saunders model than to the Weibull model.
narrate.key_results: The lowest deviance information criterion was 248.9 for the generalized Eyring-Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat gamma priors, compared with 278.4 for the best-scoring generalized Eyring-Weibull model. In pairwise comparisons, the Laplace-Metropolis estimates strongly favored the generalized Eyring-Weibull model with subjective priors, while the harmonic mean estimates favored the Weibull model with flat priors and the posterior predictive estimates gave the strongest overall support to the Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat priors. The estimated log marginal likelihoods also differed across methods: the Laplace-Metropolis estimate was highest for the Weibull model with subjective priors at -145.1006, the harmonic mean estimate was highest for the Weibull model with flat priors at -141.5369, and the posterior predictive estimate was highest for the Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat priors at -136.8164. For model fitting, the authors used one chain per model, a burn-in of 50000 iterations, and 200000 posterior samples; they report Monte Carlo error below 5% of the sample standard deviation for every parameter.

narrate.summary: This review explains how reliability engineering can be applied to artificial intelligence systems, which may fail because of software, hardware, changing operating conditions, poor data, or model weaknesses. It organizes the work using the SMART framework and describes reliability measures, failure analysis, statistical assessment, and test planning. The authors connect traditional lifetime, degradation, and recurrent-event methods to artificial intelligence and propose modelling failures as events affected by external conditions and internal model properties. The paper draws on public autonomous-vehicle testing records and an incident database, alongside illustrative classification examples and reviewed studies. It concludes that existing approaches provide useful starting points, but data scarcity and the dependence of artificial intelligence performance on its operating environment make reliable assessment difficult.

Of 126 incidents listed in the artificial intelligence incident database, the authors identify 72 as reliability-related, and 29 of those involved death or injury. In the autonomous-vehicle illustration, a flexible spline model follows the observed cumulative disengagement counts for Waymo more closely than the less flexible parametric models; estimated event rates decline over time for Waymo, Cruise, and Pony AI, while Zoox's estimated rate remains approximately level. The paper also reports a separate simulation-to-track comparison from a cited study: 62.5% of unsafe simulated tests led to unsafe track behavior, while 93.3% of safe simulated tests led to safe track behavior.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses reliability-based design optimization (RBDO), where designs must meet probability-of-failure limits despite uncertainty in design variables and parameters. Existing efficient single-loop approaches based on the first-order reliability method (FORM) can give inaccurate failure probabilities when constraints are nonlinear, leading to designs that violate reliability requirements. The authors propose the response surface single-loop (RSSL) method, which fits quadratic models to constraints and estimates failure probabilities with closed-form higher-order formulas without searching for a most probable point (MPP). They evaluate it on mathematical examples and a simulated vehicle side-impact crashworthiness problem, using computational model outputs and Monte Carlo checks. The paper reports that RSSL generally achieves more accurate reliability results than the compared FORM-based methods while using substantially fewer function evaluations than nested reliability-optimization methods.
narrate.key_results: For the first mathematical benchmark, RSSL used 24 function evaluations, compared with 1,227 for the double-loop performance measure approach; its Monte Carlo reliability indices were 2.9725 and 3.0015 against a target of 3. For the vehicle crashworthiness problem with constant standard deviations and target reliability 0.9, the authors report that RSSL alone satisfied all probabilistic constraints; the reported objective was 24.801 kg, and RSSL used 41 function evaluations versus 3,324 for the double-loop performance measure approach and 26,984 for the double-loop reliability index approach. At target reliability 0.99865, RSSL again was reported as the only compared method satisfying all constraints, with objective 30.5009 kg. In the separate nonlinear example, FORM-based methods produced substantial errors; for the more demanding failure-probability target of 0.1350%, RSSL’s reported Monte Carlo probabilities were 0.1784% and 0.1346%, with the first constraint still exceeding the target.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a preprocessing method for operational sensor data used to diagnose mechanical equipment. For the crusher, the random forest achieved a test F1-score of 0.95 and the neural network 0.91, while the support vector machine and Bayesian neural network achieved 0.97 and 0.70. narrate.summary: The paper develops adaptive multi-fidelity Gaussian process reliability analysis (AMGPRA) to estimate failure probabilities when accurate but expensive models and cheaper, less accurate models are both available. The method uses a collective learning function (CLF) to select a point and the model source together, based on how much the point is expected to improve the surrogate across a set of candidates and relative to its evaluation cost. It models limit-state responses with a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, using model outputs from three mathematical examples and a transmission-tower engineering example. The examples use simulated or computational-model data rather than observed field failure data. Overall, the proposed approach achieves similar or better accuracy at lower evaluation cost than the compared methods in most mathematical examples, and it converges for the tower example where the comparison methods do not provide results.
narrate.key_results: For the multimodal example with two model fidelities, AMGPRA using the expected feasible function cost 12.58 and has an average relative error of 0.03 percent, compared with 13.31 and 0.06 percent for multi-fidelity efficient global reliability analysis (mfEGRA). With three fidelities in that example, the reported costs are 12.32 for AMGPRA and 12.87 for mfEGRA, with 0.02 percent average relative error for both. In the ten-dimensional example, AMGPRA costs 16.8 with zero percent average relative error, compared with 18.16 and 0.02 percent for mfEGRA. For the tower example, AMGPRA estimates failure probability as 2.46 times 10 to the minus 2 at cost 28.5, using an average of 18.1 high-fidelity and 25.6 low-fidelity training points; active learning reliability method combining Kriging and Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS) did not converge even with 300 high-fidelity training points, and mfEGRA did not function properly in this case.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors use only the expected feasible function and a modified version of the U learning function as cores for the collective learning function. narrate.limitations_unstated: The main numerical comparisons use constructed mathematical models, and the tower application uses finite element outputs rather than field observations; therefore, performance on real operating data is not established. The combined model reaches 73% balanced accuracy eight weeks before failure and 82% at the end-of-life point, outperforming the resistance-only benchmark.
narrate.key_results: Using resistance and its rate of change together with stress factors, the classifier achieved 82.4% balanced accuracy at the end-of-life point and 73.0% 56 days beforehand. The benchmark achieved 66.0% at the end-of-life point and 50.7% at 56 days, while the resistance-based model without stress factors achieved 77.3% and 63.1%, respectively. Stress factors alone achieved 70.7% at the end-of-life point and 66.4% at 56 days; their average across the tested prediction horizons was 68%. narrate.summary: The paper develops the record-based transmuted generalized linear exponential distribution, extending a generalized linear exponential lifetime model. The extension is intended to address the baseline model’s inability to fit decreasing or bathtub-shaped failure rates, while also accommodating increasing failure rates. The authors derive distributional properties and several parameter-estimation methods, and assess estimation using simulated samples and a real dataset of 50 failure times measured in weeks. In the real-data comparison, the proposed distribution fits better overall than the seven alternative lifetime distributions considered. The paper provides a theoretical and numerical illustration of a flexible lifetime model, rather than a maintenance or cost optimization method.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 5,000 replicates and sample sizes of 20, 50, 100, and 200, the authors report generally small estimation biases and mean squared errors, although the results do not improve uniformly with increasing sample size. For the parameter setting alpha = 0.8, beta = 0.8, gamma = 1, and p = 0.7, the maximum-likelihood mean squared error for alpha decreases from 0.1665 at sample size 20 to 0.0784 at sample size 200. For the 50-observation failure-time dataset, the proposed model has the lowest reported negative twice log-likelihood, 258.2350, and the lowest Akaike information criterion, 266.2350, among the eight models. It also has the smallest reported Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramer-von Mises, and Anderson-Darling statistics, at 0.0869, 0.0503, and 0.2836, respectively; its corresponding reported p-values are 0.8698, 0.8768, and 0.9497.

narrate.summary: Long lifetime tests at normal operating conditions can take too much time, so the paper studies inference from tests that raise stress after a set time and stop after a specified number of failures. It models baseline lifetimes with the Gumbel Type-II distribution and represents the stress change using the tampered random variable model. The authors derive maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimates, intervals for the unknown parameters, and criteria for choosing a censoring plan. They evaluate the methods with simulated Type-II censored samples and two real datasets: fish fatigue times and patient analgesic relief times. In the reported studies, Bayesian estimates generally had lower bias and mean squared error than maximum likelihood estimates, and highest posterior density intervals were generally narrower than the alternative intervals considered.
narrate.key_results: The simulation study used 10,000 samples, with sample sizes of 50, 150, and 250; the authors report that bias and mean squared error generally decreased as sample size, number of observed failures, or stress-change time increased. They report that Bayesian estimates under linear-exponential loss generally performed better than maximum likelihood estimates in bias and mean squared error; highest posterior density intervals had the smallest average widths, while the bootstrap percentile intervals had the best coverage among the compared intervals. For the fish data, the fitted Gumbel Type-II distribution had a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance of 0.2667 and p-value 0.6781, compared with distances and p-values of 0.9833 and 2.2 × 10^-6 for Weibull, and 0.4019 and 0.0106 for exponential. narrate.summary: The paper addresses the high computational cost and possible inaccuracy of estimating rare failure probabilities with expensive engineering models, especially when the input dimension is high or failure regions are complex. It models the input-to-response relationship using a PLS-PCE surrogate constructed in a lower-dimensional linear subspace. ASSIS extends SSIS by using active learning to add informative evaluations at each sampling level, accounting for uncertainty in both the surrogate and the subspace. ASSIS’s coefficient of variation was 0.021 and relative bias was 0.030, compared with 0.625 and 0.083 for the original-model method. Across the examples, the authors report cost reductions of one to more than two orders of magnitude versus the original-model reference method at equal or lower estimation error.

narrate.summary: Estimating structural failure probabilities can require many costly model evaluations, especially for rare failures and nonlinear or multiple failure regions. The results show that no single combination is best for every problem, but using a surrogate with a sufficiently accurate reliability estimator is broadly beneficial. No strategy consistently led on every problem and metric, but polynomial-chaos Kriging, subset simulation, the deviation-number learning function, and either reliability-index bounds or the combined stopping rule were recommended overall. narrate.summary: Expensive simulator evaluations make it difficult to estimate rare failure probabilities, and a surrogate that misses parts of the failure boundary can produce a poor sampling distribution and unreliable estimates. narrate.summary: High-dimensional structural reliability calculations can require many costly model evaluations, while conventional surrogate models can lose accuracy as input dimension grows. Across these examples, the proposed method gives close agreement with the Monte Carlo benchmarks while generally using fewer model evaluations than competing accurate approaches.

For the space truss, the proposed method had a 0.6751% error with 1,000 evaluations, compared with 3.8737% for polynomial chaos expansion, 27.1076% for the first-order reliability method, and 24.7368% for the second-order reliability method. The reported results therefore show better accuracy than those comparisons in the examples studied, with relatively few model evaluations.

In the county-level outage analysis, failure rate was a statistically significant predictor at all times with outage data, while cumulative wind speed was significant at all considered times except October 12 at 23:05. narrate.summary: Disengagements during autonomous driving are used as a proxy for failures of the artificial intelligence system, with lower event rates taken to indicate greater reliability. The paper models these recurrent events with a nonhomogeneous Poisson process, adjusting the event intensity for each vehicle’s time-varying mileage. It compares established parametric models with a flexible monotone spline model, and uses likelihood estimation, bootstrap intervals, and a frailty model to assess uncertainty and differences among vehicles. The real data cover December 2017 through November 2019 for Waymo, Cruise, Pony AI, and Zoox; the paper also evaluates the methods using simulated data. The analysis finds decreasing event rates for three manufacturers, a roughly constant rate for Zoox, and little evidence of variation in event processes among vehicles within each manufacturer.
narrate.key_results: In the real-data analysis, the spline model had the lowest Akaike information criterion for Waymo, Cruise, and Pony AI: 2756.21, 2046.09, and 479.73, respectively; for Zoox its value was 688.78, slightly above the Musa-Okumoto model’s 687.69. The selected parametric models were Gompertz for Waymo and Cruise, Weibull for Pony AI, and Musa-Okumoto for Zoox. narrate.summary: This paper develops a way to rank model inputs by their influence on whether a system crosses a failure threshold, including when inputs are statistically dependent. It extends Shapley effects, which distribute shared contributions across inputs, to target sensitivity analysis (TSA) in reliability-oriented sensitivity analysis (ROSA). The authors define indices based on the variance of a pass-fail indicator and give both a Monte Carlo method and a nearest-neighbor method for estimating them. They study the method analytically and by simulation, then apply it to a river-flood model and a COVID-19 hospital-capacity model using model-generated input-output data. The indices provide nonnegative input shares that sum to one, but increasingly rare failure events can make it difficult to distinguish individual input effects from interactions.
narrate.key_results: For the flood model, the estimated failure probability was 4.5 × 10⁻³; the target Shapley effects assigned 24.3% (±1.3%) to maximum annual flow, 22.6% (±1.3%) to friction, and about 16.7% (±1%) to downstream river level, with the other inputs receiving about 12% each. These rankings differ from ordinary output-sensitivity results because the analysis concerns flood occurrence and accounts for dependent inputs. In the COVID-19 prior-input study, failure proportions across the five tested thresholds ranged from 58.1% to 2.2%; the lockdown timing input accounted for over 50% at less restrictive thresholds, while its influence fell toward an equal-share level of 1/20 as the threshold became more restrictive. In the calibrated COVID-19 study, the target effect for days until asymptomatic recovery was about 22%, and that for lockdown timing was about 15%; starting date, transmission decay rate, and initial undetected infections each had effects slightly below 10%.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that as the failure event becomes increasingly rare, all inputs tend to appear influential, making it difficult to distinguish interactions from correlation effects. The nearest-neighbor estimator can be less accurate than the sampling-based estimator and requires an independent and identically distributed input-output sample; the Monte Carlo approach can require many costly model evaluations. They also note that correlated, exogenous inputs may receive importance even without a direct causal effect on the model output.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The nearest-neighbor approach is applied to variables with different scales and units in the flood example, so distance calculations may depend strongly on input scaling; the paper does not report a scaling sensitivity check. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving sampling-based estimation with methods such as importance sampling and exploring additional given-data estimators based on copulas, squared mutual information, or random forests. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the indices against observed flood and hospital-capacity outcomes and assess whether input rankings remain stable under alternative model assumptions and operating conditions. narrate.summary: This paper presents certifiable risk-based design optimization (CRiBDO) as an alternative to reliability-based design optimization (RBDO), which constrains the probability of failure (PoF). The authors argue that PoF can miss how severe failures are and can make optimization difficult because it does not generally preserve convexity. They model risk using the superquantile, also known as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and buffered probability of failure (bPoF), which account for the size of tail outcomes. The methods are tested with simulated data on a short-column structural design and a cooling-fin thermal design, using Monte Carlo (MC) sampling and numerical optimization. The paper finds that these risk measures can produce more conservative designs, and that a convex short-column reformulation permits a global optimization guarantee for the sampled problem.
narrate.key_results: For the short-column example, the authors report that RBDO and bPoF-based optimization achieve nearly identical design frontiers when compared at similar estimated PoF or bPoF levels. With the same target failure probability of 0.05, the cooling-fin RBDO design has objective value 0.7094 and estimated PoF 0.0486, while the superquantile-constrained design has objective value 0.725 and estimated PoF 0.0195. At target failure probability 0.001, the corresponding objective values are 0.7649 for RBDO and 0.781 for the superquantile-constrained design; the latter has estimated PoF 4.3 × 10^-4. For the short-column example, convexity gives the bPoF formulation a global-optimality guarantee for its sample-average optimization problem, whereas the RBDO solutions have no such guarantee in the paper.

key_equations.name: Superquantile definition
key_equations.explanation: The superquantile is the quantile plus the expected positive excess above that quantile, scaled by one minus the risk level.

key_equations.name: Buffered probability of failure representation
key_equations.explanation: The buffered probability of failure is the minimum over auxiliary thresholds below the failure threshold of expected positive excess divided by the distance to the failure threshold.

key_equations.name: Superquantile-constrained design
key_equations.explanation: The design minimizes expected objective value subject to the superquantile of the limit-state outcome being no greater than the failure threshold.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that estimating buffered probability of failure and superquantiles can be expensive. They also note that superquantile estimates can be less stable when rare, large tail outcomes have a strong influence, and that direct optimization can be nonsmooth.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses two simulated engineering examples and does not validate the proposed designs against field or operational data, so the results do not establish performance under real-world model error. The cooling-fin case uses finite Monte Carlo samples and a nonconvex limit state, so it does not provide the same global-optimality guarantee as the convex short-column sample-average problem.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for further research on efficient estimation of buffered probability of failure and superquantiles, including Monte Carlo variance-reduction and approximation methods. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could validate the methods using measured structural and thermal field data, including tests of sensitivity to model error and uncertain input distributions. narrate.summary: This paper develops a framework for planning inspections and maintenance for structures that deteriorate and may fail, using partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) together with dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). The method represents fatigue crack growth, uncertain inspections, and possible maintenance actions, then chooses actions to reduce expected life-cycle costs. The authors test it on a simulated structural component with fatigue deterioration over a 30-year horizon, comparing policies with heuristic inspection and repair rules. The tests include both a traditional setting and a more detailed setting with two inspection methods and two repair options. The POMDP policies achieve lower expected costs than the tested heuristic policies in the reported cases.
narrate.key_results: In the traditional setting, the finite-horizon POMDP cost was 12.45 for one experiment, compared with 17.06 for the optimized equidistant-inspection heuristic and 16.69 for the optimized failure-probability-threshold heuristic; these heuristics cost 37 percent and 34 percent more, respectively. In a separate traditional experiment, the POMDP cost was 58.35, compared with 69.17 and 65.62 for the two heuristic policies, which were 18 percent and 12 percent higher. In the detailed setting, the finite-horizon POMDP cost was 12.26, while the best listed heuristic cost was 13.66, or 11 percent more; the other tested heuristic costs ranged up to 18.08, or 47 percent more. For the discretization comparison, the deterioration-rate model with 930 states had a reported normalized error of 2.1 × 10⁻⁴, while the parametric model required 16,000 states for a normalized error of 4.3 × 10⁻⁴.

narrate.summary: This review surveys how machine learning (ML) is being used in reliability engineering and safety, rather than presenting a new predictive model or experiment. It discusses problems such as inaccurate remaining useful life (RUL) estimates, missed or late fault detection, false alarms, and the difficulty of handling complex systems and large data sets. The reviewed approaches model or predict degradation, faults, anomalies, health states, and maintenance or inspection decisions using supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning. The authors describe applications involving equipment and structures, spacecraft telemetry, accident records, and simulated or measured engineering data; the review itself does not analyze one original data set. Its main conclusion is that these methods offer useful opportunities, while uncertainty, false alarms, and deployment challenges remain important barriers.
narrate.key_results: The review reports an example graph-based fault detection and classification method for solar photovoltaic arrays that achieved 99% accuracy under real working conditions while using less than 2% labeled data. In a reviewed analysis of spacecraft anomalies, 41% of the expert-labeled anomalies were contextual, illustrating why fixed-limit alarms may miss relevant patterns. A reviewed recurrent-network application detected anomalies across more than 700 spacecraft telemetry channels, but high false-positive rates remained an obstacle to deployment. These are results from selected studies, not pooled estimates or a head-to-head evaluation conducted by this review.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say their survey is not exhaustive and that their list of future opportunities is subjective and deliberately brief. They also exclude the reliability and safety of machine learning and artificial intelligence systems from the review, noting that this topic warrants separate treatment.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review does not describe a reproducible literature search or systematic criteria for selecting studies, so relevant work may be missing and the selection may be biased. Results come from heterogeneous applications and study designs, without a common evaluation protocol or quantitative synthesis, so claims of superior performance across methods cannot be directly compared.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify opportunities in uncertainty quantification and deployment, fleet-level and system-of-systems health management, machine learning for accident databases and safety management, wearable sensing for predictive safety, and deep Gaussian processes and generative adversarial networks. They also propose examining the reliability and safety of machine learning and artificial intelligence systems in future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare methods using shared benchmarks and report calibrated uncertainty, false-alarm burden, and operational costs alongside predictive accuracy. They could also test transfer across equipment types and operating conditions and validate performance prospectively using field data, especially where failures are rare and maintenance decisions affect system-level risk.

narrate.summary: The paper models time to failure of downhole safety valves, where failure rates do not always remain proportional over time and unobserved differences among valves may matter. It extends the generalized time-dependent logistic model by allowing covariates to affect the time effect and, when supported by the data, including gamma frailty to represent unobserved heterogeneity. The authors analyze confidential operational records from Petrobras oil wells in Brazil, with 366 valve records and 83 observed failures; missing covariate data require separate analyses for four variable groups. Their models identify associations between failure time and flow, valve, environmental, and operating characteristics, and the diagnostics indicate generally reasonable fit while also finding influential records. The paper reports reliability estimates and covariate effects, but does not report a predictive error comparison against competing methods.
narrate.key_results: Of 366 valve records, 83 (22.68%) were failures and the remainder were censored; removing records with missing explanatory data across all variables would leave only 54, so the authors fit separate models by covariate group. The valve-characteristics analysis selected the gamma-frailty model, with an estimated frailty variance of 12.3951 and standard error 3.5735, indicating unobserved heterogeneity in that group. The selected factors across the four groups included hydrogen sulfide and basic sediment and water; pressure class, manufacturer, and family; operating unit, closed well temperature, and water column; and well flowing pressure. For the operation group, the hazard ratio comparing the first and third quartiles of well flowing pressure was initially close to 2 and remained above 1.5 at 20 years; the residual plots were reported to show generally good agreement with the assumed distribution, although influence diagnostics identified cases that could change estimates.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of choosing inspections and maintenance actions when infrastructure deterioration is uncertain, observations are incomplete, and resources or risk are constrained. It models the problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and uses deep reinforcement learning to learn decentralized policies for components or other control units. Its Deep Decentralized Multi-agent Actor Critic method combines neural-network policies, experience replay, state augmentation for budget limits, and Lagrangian relaxation for risk constraints. The method is evaluated in simulations of a stochastic, partially observable, ten-component deteriorating system over 50 decision steps, with modeled observations and deterioration rather than field measurements. The learned policy outperforms the tested baseline policies in the unconstrained comparison, while stricter budget or risk limits change inspection and maintenance choices and can increase risk or cost.
narrate.key_results: In the unconstrained simulation, the best optimized baseline policy had a life-cycle cost about 42% higher than the learned Deep Decentralized Multi-agent Actor Critic policy. For five-year budget limits, policies with limits above 25% of system rebuild cost practically converged to the unconstrained solution; below 10%, replacement actions were infeasible because replacement cost 10% of rebuild cost. For life-cycle risk limits, constrained results practically converged to the unconstrained solution above a tolerance of 2.75 times rebuild cost, while the authors describe policies below 2.0 times rebuild cost as practically unrealistic because of frequent restorations or replacements. The study also reports that tighter budgets reduce inspections and can increase risk disproportionately, while stricter risk limits require more maintenance and increase total life-cycle cost.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of pricing full-service maintenance contracts when machines have different maintenance needs and costs. It models recurring minor failures, catastrophic failures, failure types, and maintenance costs using machine characteristics, then estimates their parameters from event and cost histories. The authors use simulated data for a portfolio of 5,000 machines and evaluate prices against costs observed in a later, out-of-time period. A single uniform price can overcharge low-risk machines and undercharge maintenance-heavy ones, potentially encouraging low-risk customers to leave. The main finding is that prices differentiated by machine risk better reflect cost differences and reduce this adverse-selection concern.
narrate.key_results: For a two-year contract horizon, the out-of-time loss ratios were 0.992 for the uniform tariff, 0.989 for the tariff using fixed machine characteristics, and 0.994 for the tariff using both fixed and time-varying characteristics; all were close to break-even. The Gini indices were 0.033, 0.128, and 0.129, respectively, indicating substantially greater cost differentiation for the two risk-based tariffs than for the uniform tariff. The advantage of including the time-varying characteristic over using fixed characteristics alone was minor in this experiment. In 250 simulation replications with 1,000 machines per replication, average parameter estimates were close to the simulation settings; for example, the baseline scale was 0.496 versus 0.5, and the catastrophic-failure scale was 0.200 versus 0.2.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses structural failure-probability estimates that are difficult or expensive to obtain because the performance function or its components require costly evaluations. It models aleatory variability in structural inputs separately from epistemic uncertainty that can be reduced by experiments, including for hierarchical models with expensive intermediate components. It proposes a sequential, one-step-look-ahead experimental design method that combines an unscented transform with Monte Carlo importance sampling and prunes samples expected to have little influence. The method is evaluated using simulated examples, including reliability benchmarks and a synthetic corroded-pipeline case, rather than field data. The examples show that the approach can estimate failure probabilities with relatively few evaluations, while the paper also identifies limits to its one-step strategy and uncertainty approximations.
narrate.key_results: For the four-branch benchmark, the method used 65 evaluations at the 2.5% stopping threshold and reported a failure-probability interval of 4.347 to 4.444 times 10 to the minus 3; the paper’s Monte Carlo reference was 4.416 times 10 to the minus 3. At the 10% threshold, it used 35 evaluations and reported an interval of 4.163 to 4.547 times 10 to the minus 3; the authors report that a conservative estimate from this run had less than 3% relative error, decreasing to 0.65% after 30 additional evaluations. In the hierarchical benchmark, the method converged after 10 total evaluations of the two expensive components, with 2 evaluations of one component and 8 of the other; the reference failure probability was about 8.1 times 10 to the minus 3. In the synthetic pipeline example, the target-based stopping rule was reached after 25 iterations in the illustrated run; across 100 runs, the averages were 23 additional evaluations of the capacity model, 10 observations of model discrepancy, and 2 defect-depth measurements when starting with one initial capacity-model observation and stopping at the target.

narrate.key_results: The proposed model reports root mean squared error (RMSE) values of 12.14, 20.85, 13.23, and 21.34 on datasets FD001 through FD004, respectively; the corresponding GRU-based metric-regression baseline reports 15.36, 22.43, 12.52, and 22.96. Its average rank is 2.0 for RMSE and 2.25 for the timeliness score, compared with 3.75 for both measures for that baseline. The proposed model's timeliness scores are 212, 3,196, 370, and 2,795, compared with 481, 3,391, 339, and 2,964 for the baseline, so it is better on FD001, FD002, and FD004 but worse on FD003. narrate.summary: The paper addresses forecasting how an equipment health indicator will change after only its early-life measurements are available, so that remaining useful life (RUL) can be estimated. It chooses the candidate with the smallest root mean squared error (RMSE) against the observed portion, then estimates RUL from the forecasted threshold crossing. The evaluation uses four sensor-derived indicators from two subsets of the Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) turbofan benchmark, with held-out run-to-failure engines truncated to simulate partial observations. The proposed method outperforms the tested alternatives on both health-indicator forecasting and RUL estimation in these experiments.
narrate.key_results: Across the tested cases, the authors report an average 24% improvement in health-indicator forecasting and an average 20% improvement in RUL estimation over the best baseline. The reported health-indicator forecasting improvements range from 7.04% to 43.31%, and the RUL improvements range from 6.18% to 36.12%. The comparisons include a functional-data empirical Bayesian method, linear regression forecasting, and nearest-neighbor scenario matching with and without smoothing; nearest-neighbor methods were generally the next-best performers. The authors attribute the poorer empirical Bayesian results to a violated assumption behind its posterior calculation, and the linear regression baseline to windowing curves and treating windows from the same engine as independent.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how to compare the lifetimes of k-out-of-n systems, whose lifetimes are represented by order statistics of component lifetimes. It does not model degradation or optimize a maintenance or design decision; instead, it derives conditions under which one system lifetime has second-order stochastic dominance (SSD) over another. The method uses assumptions about the shape of the component lifetime distribution, including the increasing failure rate (IFR) property, together with conditions on ranks and sample sizes. The authors also propose a nonparametric test of distribution-shape conditions and assess it using simulated samples, alongside theoretical derivations and numerical examples. The main finding is a flexible set of sufficient comparison conditions, with broader assumptions about component distributions generally requiring more restrictive rank and sample-size conditions.
narrate.key_results: The main theoretical result gives sufficient conditions for SSD between order statistics using their ranks, sample sizes, and a relative-convexity condition on the parent distribution; the paper develops four classes of parent distributions, including the IFR class. For the test of odds-convexity, the authors simulated 3,000 samples at each sample size from 10 through 30 and 1,000 samples at each sample size from 40 through 100 to obtain reference quantiles. In a separate simulation of 100 samples per distribution, the test accepted the odds-convexity null hypothesis for 59% of gamma samples with shape 0.5 at sample size 100, while for Pareto samples with shape 0.5 the acceptance rate was 11% at sample size 100, using a significance level of 0.1. These simulations evaluate the proposed shape test, not estimation accuracy or prediction error, and the paper reports no field-data comparison.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors describe the proposed tests as conservative. Their simulations also show limited detection of non-odds-convexity for gamma samples with shape 0.5, although the rejection rate improves as sample size increases for the Pareto samples with shape 0.5.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The system comparisons assume independent, identically distributed component lifetimes from a common parent distribution in the one-sample setting; dependence between components and changing operating conditions are not addressed. The test is evaluated by simulation rather than on field lifetime data, and the comparisons rely on distribution-shape assumptions that may be difficult to establish from finite or censored reliability data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to increasing and convex order. They state that this would involve other classes of parent distributions, such as distributions with decreasing failure rate.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could adapt the comparison and testing procedures to dependent component lifetimes, covariates, multiple operating conditions, and censored observations, then validate them using field reliability data. It could also connect the lifetime comparisons to system-level decisions such as inspection, replacement, or design selection.

narrate.summary: Repeated evaluation of a system’s limit-state function can make reliability analysis costly, particularly when that function is defined by a differential equation. The paper models the system response with a physics-informed deep neural network (PI-DNN), trained to satisfy the governing ordinary or partial differential equation rather than to fit simulation-generated response data. The method uses collocation points and automatic differentiation to calculate equation residuals, then optimizes the network parameters to reduce those residuals. It is tested on three numerical benchmarks: a stochastic decay equation, viscous Burgers’ equation, and a cell-signalling cascade, using simulated benchmark results for comparison. The reported estimates are close to the benchmarks while requiring no repeated system simulations to produce the PI-DNN reliability estimates.
narrate.key_results: For the stochastic decay benchmark, the PI-DNN estimated a failure probability of 0.0035, compared with the exact value of 0.003539; the paper reports a 0.06% reliability-index error. For viscous Burgers’ equation, its failure-probability estimate was 0.0999 versus 0.1037 from Monte Carlo simulation, with a reported reliability-index error of 1.70%; the Monte Carlo benchmark used 10,000 finite-element solver runs. For the cell-signalling cascade, the PI-DNN estimate was 0.0459, matching the reported Monte Carlo estimate of 0.0459, which used 10,000 solver runs. The PI-DNN required zero system simulations to generate these estimates, although it still required collocation points and neural-network training.

narrate.summary: One-shot devices are inspected at set times, so the data show whether each unit has failed by inspection or has survived beyond it, rather than its exact failure time. The paper addresses how conventional maximum likelihood inference can lose robustness when some inspection-time and stress-condition cells are contaminated. narrate.key_results: The simulation study used 1,000 simulated samples and found that estimators with positive tuning parameter values were generally more robust to contaminated cells than the maximum likelihood estimator; estimation errors decreased as sample sizes increased. For contaminated data, the conventional Wald test had empirical levels far above the nominal 0.05 level, whereas the robust tests stayed close to nominal levels and retained useful power. In the electric-current example, which included 120 devices, the proportional hazards model's best reported fit was at tuning parameter 0.5, with discrepancy statistic 1.40 and p-value 0.942. At that setting, estimated reliabilities at the three reported inspection times were 0.868, 0.816, and 0.782.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a Bayesian method for estimating recurrent failures in multiple repairable systems when different failure causes may be dependent. Each cause-specific failure stream is modelled with a power law process (PLP), and a shared frailty term represents system-to-system heterogeneity and induces dependence between causes. The frailty distribution is estimated flexibly using a Dirichlet process mixture (DPM), with a hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) procedure; closed-form posterior estimates are available for the PLP parameters. The method is evaluated using simulated failure histories and automobile warranty data with three failure causes. The analyses indicate accurate parameter estimates in the simulations and meaningful heterogeneity and dependence in the automobile data.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 50,000 replications and 10, 50, or 100 systems, parameter-estimate biases were generally near zero, and mean squared errors (MSEs) decreased as the number of systems increased. For most PLP parameters, reported 95 percent interval coverage was around 0.94 to 0.95; coverage for frailty variance was lower in some small-sample settings, including 0.8395 when the variance was 0.5 and there were 10 systems. The warranty analysis used 439 automobiles, including 267 with no failures; the observed failure counts were 76, 87, and 111 for the three causes. Estimated shape parameters were 0.300, 0.409, and 0.698, all below 1, and the estimated frailty variance was 1.755 with a reported 95 percent interval of 1.050 to 2.777. The paper does not report a comparison against an alternative estimation method.

narrate.summary: The paper studies online detection and classification of unusual logging activity in a computing center, rather than predicting equipment lifetime or physical failures. It models the severity of anomalous time windows with two evolving granular classifiers, which update their rules as log data arrive. The data are operational event-oriented logs from the StoRM back-end service at the Bologna computing center, converted into five activity measures and weak labels from a control chart. Each dataset contains 1,436 instances, and the analysis compares window lengths of 5, 15, 30, and 60 minutes. Accuracy generally improves with longer windows, and the evolving granular neural network achieves the strongest compact-model result at 96.17% accuracy with 60-minute windows.
narrate.key_results: For 60-minute windows, the evolving granular neural network reached 96.17% accuracy with a standard deviation of 0.78 percentage points, an average of 10.35 rules, and a processing time of 0.18 seconds; the fuzzy-set-based evolving model reached 85.64% accuracy with a standard deviation of 3.69 points, 12.63 rules, and 0.18 seconds. At 5 minutes, their reported accuracies were 85.00% and 67.27%, respectively. When the number of rules was not tightly constrained, the fuzzy-set-based model reached 96.1% accuracy with about 40 rules, while the neural network reached 96.2% with about 10 rules. The authors report that the fuzzy-set-based model slightly outperformed the neural network in detecting the highest-severity class, although the neural network had higher overall accuracy.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors characterize the automatically generated control-chart labels as weak and the classification problem as unbalanced. narrate.summary: Reliability-based design optimization can become computationally expensive when reliability constraints must be evaluated repeatedly during optimization. This paper proposes approximating the failure probability function (FPF) by estimating the density of design points associated with failure, using iterative partitions that focus additional sampling on low-density regions. Bayesian sequential partitioning estimates density within regions, and regression is used to smooth the result. The method is demonstrated with simulated data for a cantilever box beam, where failure occurs if its first natural frequency lies between 550 and 600 radians per second. The authors report that the resulting probability contours agree with direct simulation and that the method uses far fewer model evaluations in this example.
narrate.key_results: For the beam illustration, the authors report 36,000 model evaluations for the proposed method, compared with 5.68 × 10^7 for direct Monte Carlo simulation across the design grid. The probability contours from the proposed method were described as consistent with the direct Monte Carlo results, although no numerical error metric was reported. At allowable failure probabilities of 0.01, 10^-3, and 10^-4, the proposed method gave optimal mean width and height values of [30.0, 32.9], [30.0, 31.5], and [30.0, 30.4] millimeters, respectively; the corresponding direct simulation results were [30.0, 32.7], [30.0, 31.4], and [30.0, 30.4] millimeters.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that selecting a regression function through model comparison is beyond the scope of the paper. They do not otherwise identify specific limitations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is a single simulated example with two design variables, and the paper reports no numerical error metric or validation against field or experimental data. narrate.summary: Estimating very small failure probabilities with costly engineering models can require many model evaluations. This paper proposes REAK, which uses a Kriging surrogate, prioritizes important parts of the input space, and estimates an upper bound on the failure-probability error to guide stopping. The method is evaluated using simulated model outputs for four reliability examples, including nonlinear systems with two, six, and nine random variables. Its estimated error bound is compared with observed error across repeated simulations and is generally conservative. The authors report fewer model evaluations than AK-MCS and ISKRA for most tested error targets, with the largest reported savings reaching 59 percent.
narrate.key_results: At a 5 percent target error rate, the paper reports that REAK reduced performance-function evaluations relative to AK-MCS and ISKRA by 52 percent and 50 percent for the four-boundary series example, 56 percent and 59 percent for the modified Rastrigin example, 51 percent and 50 percent for the nonlinear oscillator, and 33 percent and 21 percent for the cantilever tube. In 50 repeated simulations of the first example at that target, REAK averaged 58.36 evaluations, compared with 74.60 for ISKRA and 90.96 for AK-MCS. Across the examples, the estimated maximum error rate was generally larger than the observed error rate; reported probabilities that the bound covered the true error were near or above the nominal 95 percent in the cases discussed. For the cantilever example at a 1 percent target, however, REAK averaged 80.42 evaluations, more than ISKRA at 75.64.

key_equations.name: Relative error rate
key_equations.explanation: Epsilon is the relative error rate, the hatted failure probability is the estimate from the surrogate, and the failure probability marked MCS is the estimate from crude Monte Carlo simulation on the same candidate samples.

key_equations.name: Error-bound stopping rule
key_equations.explanation: The hatted maximum epsilon is REAK's estimated upper bound on the error rate, and target epsilon is the user-prescribed error threshold that the bound must not exceed.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that REAK is challenging to apply to very high-dimensional problems because Kriging requires repeated inversions of large covariance matrices. The method assumes that wrong-sign predictions at candidate points are independent; accounting for correlations may improve accuracy for higher error thresholds but would increase computational demands.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated benchmark outputs rather than field or operational data, so the reported efficiency and error coverage are not demonstrated on real infrastructure models. The comparisons also rely on generated candidate samples and particular Kriging and sampling settings, leaving performance under different input distributions and modeling choices untested.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying dimension-reduction techniques for high-dimensional problems and considering correlations among wrong-sign predictions. They also suggest combining REAK with importance sampling or subset simulation, and selecting multiple training points in parallel using unsupervised learning.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using field-informed or experimentally measured structural data, including uncertainty in the model itself rather than only uncertainty in its inputs. Further work could also test how REAK behaves for time-dependent failure, competing failure mechanisms, and system-level reliability, then connect its error target to engineering decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper models a multi-component series system in which each component can be replaced individually after inspection, but failures between inspections may remain undetected and cause downtime. It represents gradual wear with gamma processes and adds shock damage to each component; in turn, accumulated degradation and previous shocks raise the shock arrival rate. The authors optimize each next inspection interval using the starting degradation of the components and a cost rate that includes inspection, replacement, and downtime costs. They illustrate the method with simulated results for a jet pipe servo-valve, using spool and sleeve components and 100,000 Monte Carlo replications. The mutually dependent model gives lower reliability and shorter optimal inspection intervals than the independent-shock comparison model.
narrate.key_results: The reliability curves show lower reliability for the mutually dependent model than for the model with independent Poisson shock arrivals; the paper reports this result qualitatively rather than as a single accuracy or error measure. With both components starting at zero degradation, the optimal interval is 1.432 times 10 to the minus 4 for the independent model and 0.741 times 10 to the minus 4 for the mutually dependent model. For the scenario with spool degradation 4.8 and sleeve degradation 5.5, the reported intervals are 0.023 times 10 to the minus 4 and 0.009 times 10 to the minus 4, respectively.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how to estimate software reliability growth when failures follow a power law process (PLP), a non-homogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with a time-varying failure rate. It estimates the shape parameter using Bayesian analysis with the Higgins-Tsokos (H-T) loss function and examines several parametric and kernel-based prior distributions. The authors compare the Bayesian estimates with maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs) using simulated failure times and Crow’s 40 observed failure times from a developmental test. The comparisons use mean squared error (MSE) for the parameters and relative efficiency for intensity estimates. Across the tested simulations, the Bayesian approach generally has lower estimation error, but its results depend on the selected prior.
narrate.key_results: For the simulation with sample size 40 and scale parameter theta equal to 1.7441, the MSE for the Bayesian shape estimate with the Burr prior was 0.000516057, compared with 0.0110573 for the MLE. With true beta equal to 0.7054 and sample size 20, the reported average Bayesian estimate was 0.675263, compared with 0.784026 for the MLE; the true value was 0.7054. For the estimated intensity, the reported relative efficiency ratio for the Bayesian estimate versus the MLE was 0.0761919, with values below 1 favoring the Bayesian estimate under the paper’s criterion. For Crow’s failure data, the Bayesian estimates were beta equal to 0.501199 and theta equal to 2.07144; the paper reports a fitted intensity of 0.347933 times time to the power of negative 0.498801.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not list study limitations explicitly. They do state that the Bayesian estimate is sensitive to prior selection and recommend Jeffreys or kernel priors when prior knowledge of the shape parameter is lacking.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data demonstration uses one set of 40 failure times from a developmental test, so it does not establish performance across different software systems or field operating conditions. The simulations generate data under the assumed power law process and use a Burr distribution to generate the shape parameter, limiting how broadly the comparisons test model misspecification; the paper also does not report the computational cost of its numerical integration.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors do not propose specific future research. Their stated practical recommendation is to use Jeffreys or kernel prior distributions when prior knowledge of the shape parameter is unavailable.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method on independent field software failure records and test its robustness when the failure process departs from the power law assumption. It could also assess operating-condition covariates, compare prior choices using external validation, and connect reliability estimates to software release or maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: Expensive evaluations of engineering performance functions make conventional reliability analysis costly, while first-order approximations can be inaccurate for nonlinear problems or multiple failure regions. The paper proposes Surrogates for Importance Sampling (S4IS), which adaptively selects evaluations of the original function in two stages: first to identify failure regions, then to focus on important regions and estimate failure probability more accurately. The method uses importance sampling (IS) and is designed to work with different surrogate types, although the examples use Gaussian processes (GPs). It is evaluated in five numerical examples using simulated inputs and computational model outputs, including system reliability, nonlinear limit states, rare failures, and problems with up to 50 random variables. Across these examples, S4IS generally achieves low estimation error with fewer evaluations than the adaptive Kriging-based importance-sampling method (AK-IS), and is more reliable than the first-order reliability method (FORM) in the challenging cases studied.
narrate.key_results: In the four-region series-system example, S4IS estimated failure probability with 0.5% relative error using 60.6 performance-function evaluations; the reported coefficient of variation (CoV) was 1.06%, compared with 73.6% relative error for AK-IS. For the nonlinear oscillator, S4IS had 0.9% relative error and CoV below 5.0% with 53.3 evaluations, about half the AK-IS evaluation count. In the example with 50 random variables, S4IS estimated failure probability with 1.0% relative error and CoV below 5.0% using 168.6 evaluations, compared with 1,845.2 evaluations for AK-IS. For the smallest failure probability reported, 9.485 × 10⁻⁷, S4IS achieved 4.7% relative error with 118.6 evaluations; the paper reports that FORM and AK-IS were inaccurate in that example.
