narrate.summary: Traditional pavement condition inspections rely on visual surveys, which the paper identifies as a safety concern and a possible source of human error. The authors model the pavement condition index (PCI) from pavement deflection readings collected with a falling weight deflectometer (FWD), rather than estimating the score directly from a visual survey. They compare multilayer perceptron (MLP) and radial basis function (RBF) neural networks, then combine their predictions in a committee machine intelligent system (CMIS). The data are measurements from 236 flexible-pavement segments on the Tehran-Qom freeway in Iran, with PCI scores calculated for those segments. The combined model had the best overall error results among the models tested, supporting the potential use of deflection data to estimate PCI in this case study.
narrate.key_results: For the full dataset, the CMIS had an average percent relative error (APRE) of 2.3303%, an average absolute percent relative error (AAPRE) of 11.6768%, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 12.005653, and a standard error (SD) of 0.021081. The authors report that these overall results were better than those of the individual models; for example, the MLP optimized with Levenberg-Marquardt had an overall AAPRE of 14.4877% and RMSE of 14.499431. On the test data, the CMIS had an AAPRE of 11.9464% and RMSE of 11.807884. The authors also report that the largest relative error for the CMIS was below 33%.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal designs for accelerated degradation testing (ADT) when the goal is to estimate lifetime quantiles from degradation measurements rather than observed failure times. It models one response with a gamma degradation process and extends the method to two independent failure modes, using either two gamma processes or a gamma process together with a linear mixed-effects model (LMEM). The designs allocate test units across stress levels while keeping stress constant for each unit and using repeated measurements over time. The authors optimize the asymptotic variance of estimated failure-time quantiles using locally specified model parameters and a numerical multiplicative algorithm. narrate.summary: This paper presents an extension of Attribute Oriented Induction (AOI) for predictive maintenance of turbine engines. The method groups sensor readings into weighted clusters and turns those weights into a function intended to track machine wear. An Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) chart detects changes, while a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model forecasts the function and Western Electric Rules (WER) determine when an anomaly is reached and estimate Remaining Useful Life (RUL). The experiments use simulated turbine-engine data from a public NASA Ames dataset, with 100 training runs ending after failure and 100 test runs ending before failure. The authors report that changes were detected before failure in all cases, while RUL accuracy was weaker when change was detected very early.
narrate.key_results: The selected fourth Western Electric Rule had a mean absolute error of 6.26 cycles and a mean squared error of 72.74 when estimating failure timing; the corresponding errors for the first, second, and third rules were 56.0 and 8518.48, 33.25 and 4125.35, and 17.55 and 1084.13. The LSTM prediction of the quantification function had a reported root mean square error of 0.036021. For the overall system, the reported RUL mean absolute error was 39.02 cycles, improving to 13.30 when considering only runs whose change point occurred after the first 40 cycles. Change points were detected before failure in 100% of cases. The paper does not report a comparison against a separate prognostics method or a field-data evaluation.

narrate.summary: Multifidelity Efficient Global Reliability Analysis (mfEGRA) addresses the high computational cost of estimating failure probability when evaluations of the most accurate model are expensive. It builds a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate that combines high- and low-fidelity models, then adaptively chooses both where to sample and which model to evaluate. The method uses the expected feasibility function (EFF) to target the failure boundary and a cost-adjusted, weighted lookahead information gain to choose an information source. The authors test it on an analytic multimodal problem and on simulated acoustic-horn models, including a rarer failure case with manufacturing uncertainty. In these examples, mfEGRA reaches the reported accuracy with fewer equivalent high-fidelity evaluations than single-fidelity EGRA, with savings depending on model discrepancy and relative evaluation costs.
narrate.key_results: On the analytic problem, mfEGRA reached median relative failure-probability error below 10^-3 at a cost of 26 equivalent high-fidelity evaluations, compared with 48 for EGRA, a reported 46% reduction. For the three-dimensional acoustic horn, it required 19 evaluations versus 25 for EGRA to reach the same error threshold, a 24% reduction; restricting candidate locations to pre-drawn Monte Carlo samples increased the saving to 45%, with 12 versus 22 evaluations. For the rarer four-dimensional acoustic-horn case, the methods required 25 versus 48 evaluations, a reported 48% saving, to reach median relative error below 10^-3. The analytic results used 100 initial designs for comparison, and each acoustic-horn comparison used 10 initial designs.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for grouping subjects according to their underlying lifetime distributions, including settings where termination events are right-censored or cannot be observed. A neural network assigns subjects to clusters using their covariates and activity measurements from an initial period, while training aims to make the clusters’ empirical lifetime distributions as distinct as possible. The method estimates those distributions with a modified Kaplan–Meier estimator and uses a bounded Kuiper-test p-value as its clustering objective. The authors evaluate it on simulated data, Friendster activity records, and patient data from MIMIC III. They report that the proposed method generally produces more distinct and more predictive lifetime clusters than the comparison methods, while a different divergence baseline can produce empty or very small clusters.
narrate.key_results: On the synthetic three-cluster dataset, DeepCLife with the Kuiper bound achieved a C-index of 68.96% and an adjusted Rand index of 73.61%, compared with 63.77% and 47.67% for the strongest listed alternative on those measures. With four Friendster clusters, the corresponding results were 77.04%, 18.99%, and 59,236.36, compared with the strongest alternative values of 76.55%, 20.64%, and 40,703.01. On MIMIC III with two clusters, it achieved a C-index of 66.30% and a logrank score of 20,525.26, versus 64.93% and 17,193.38 for the strongest comparison; its Brier score was 15.50%, while another method scored 15.03%. narrate.summary: The paper proposes ASTPA, a method for estimating small failure probabilities in reliability problems. It guides sampling toward likely failure regions by combining the original parameter distribution with a likelihood based on the limit-state function, then adjusts the estimate using inverse importance sampling. The sampling uses HMCMC, including a Quasi-Newton preconditioned version intended to improve exploration in high-dimensional problems. The authors test the approach on four simulated structural reliability benchmarks, including static limit-state examples and dynamic oscillator models. They report that the Quasi-Newton version often estimates failure probabilities more accurately and with less variation than the comparison methods at similar numbers of model evaluations.
narrate.key_results: Results are based on 500 independent simulations per example. For the undamped oscillator with an exact failure probability of 1.55E-8, the Quasi-Newton method estimated 1.51E-8 with a coefficient of variation of 0.15; the standard Hamiltonian method estimated 1.52E-8 with 0.21, while the two Subset Simulation estimates were 1.67E-8 and 1.50E-8 with coefficients of variation of 0.77 and 0.70. For the 101-variable white-noise oscillator with an exact probability of 2.53E-6, the Quasi-Newton estimate was 2.55E-6 with a coefficient of variation of 0.24, compared with 2.57E-6 and 0.30 for standard Hamiltonian sampling and 2.58E-6 and 0.32 for uniform-proposal Subset Simulation. In the two-variable parabolic example, the Quasi-Newton estimate was 3.47E-5 with a coefficient of variation of 0.39, compared with 3.86E-5 and 0.35 for standard Hamiltonian sampling and coefficients of variation of 0.62 and 0.65 for the two Subset Simulation variants.

narrate.summary: This chapter reviews reliability methods for data that include covariates changing over time, alongside methods for planning accelerated tests. It covers failure-time prediction, degradation, and recurrent events, and explains how covariate histories can be incorporated into each type of model. The examples use field records from office machines and repairable industrial systems, outdoor coating measurements, and laboratory fatigue tests on glass fiber. It also describes Bayesian sequential test planning, which updates test conditions as results arrive. In the fatigue-test illustration, this planning approach produced a substantially lower average estimated variance than a local design based on a small amount of historical data.
narrate.key_results: In the office-machine data, 69 of 1,800 units failed during 70 weeks; predictions account for the 1,731 units still at risk. The coating example used 36 specimens observed outdoors for about 5 years, and its fitted model predicted that most of the illustrated population would fail between 50 and 150 days in service at the chosen failure threshold. The repairable-system example included 203 units followed for 110 months, with 219 component events and 44 subsystem events; its retrospective predictions for the final 15 months tracked the observed cumulative counts within the displayed 95% prediction intervals, and its 30-month projection ranged from 62 to 90 component events at a 95% confidence level. In 100 fatigue-test simulations, the sequential Bayesian design had an average asymptotic variance of 0.6048, compared with 4.0337 for the local design; the sequential design allocated 8 and 4 units to standardized stress levels 0.35 and 0.75.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a structured-effect neural network (SENN) to predict remaining useful life (RUL) while preserving interpretable components of the forecast. It combines a population-level lifetime distribution, a linear contribution from current sensor readings, and a recurrent neural network that uses sensor history to model additional patterns. The authors estimate model parameters using variational Bayesian inference, allowing uncertainty in parameter estimates to be represented. They compare the method with lifetime-distribution models and machine-learning approaches using a public simulated aircraft-engine dataset with 200 engines and 21 sensors. The proposed method is more accurate than the distribution-based and traditional machine-learning comparisons, while a long short-term memory model has the lowest reported prediction error overall.
narrate.key_results: The best SENN specification, using a log-normal lifetime component and engineered sensor features, achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 13.267 cycles, compared with 27.409 cycles for the log-normal conditional-expectation baseline, a reported error reduction of 51.60 percent. It also improved on the best traditional machine-learning result, the feature-engineered random forest at 17.793 cycles, by a reported 25.44 percent. The long short-term memory (LSTM) model had the lowest MAE overall at 11.188 cycles; the best SENN therefore did not outperform the strongest deep-learning comparison. For the illustrated SENN decomposition, the reported component scores were 0.175 for the lifetime-distribution component, 0.408 for the linear component, and 0.064 for the recurrent component.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that variational Bayesian inference is more computationally costly than Bayesian approximation via dropout. They explain that dropout does not provide uncertainty estimates for the model's coefficients or allow prior information about those coefficients, which is why they chose variational inference. They also report that a variant with an extra recurrent-component weight overfit and that two-stage estimation performed worse than their proposed joint approach.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Evaluation is confined to one simulated aircraft-engine benchmark, with 200 engines and a predetermined training and test split; the paper does not validate the approach on field data or other equipment. Sensor names are anonymized, and the study does not report an assessment of how uncertainty or errors generalize across independent real-world fleets. The method predicts RUL rather than evaluating failure probabilities or maintenance costs, and the paper does not describe handling censored lifetimes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors do not set out a specific future-work agenda. They discuss dropout-based Bayesian approximation as an alternative, but explain why it does not meet their requirements for coefficient uncertainty and prior information.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method on field data, including censored lifetimes and different operating environments, and to test whether its uncertainty estimates remain calibrated across fleets. Further work could examine additional failure mechanisms and covariates, and connect RUL forecasts to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions that account for costs and consequences.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the extra travel delay caused when road maintenance reduces traffic capacity, and the need to choose a start time that limits that delay. It proposes collecting real-time traffic status from commercial map services, calibrating map status categories to vehicle speed, and converting speed to traffic volume with a practical speed and flow model. The resulting traffic estimates and work-zone capacity are used in a queue-based delay calculation for candidate start times. The authors evaluate the method with field observations, traffic videos, and map data from a highway in Switzerland and a road-maintenance case in Shanghai. In the Shanghai case, the method identifies a start-time window that reduces modeled delay, while the paper does not report a direct comparative error or cost benchmark.
narrate.key_results: For the Swiss E60 highway, the classical speed and flow fit had a reported R-squared value of 0.96. The practical model estimated traffic at 1,688 passenger-car units per hour per lane during congestion, and upstream observations were used to check that estimate. In the Shanghai case, an eight-hour work zone starting at 8 p.m. produced a modeled total delay of 66,885 hours. Comparing candidate start times, the authors found the minimum-delay window was between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m.; they report no numerical comparison against another optimization method.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses how manufacturers can choose the number of products to test when demonstrating that reliability meets a target. The approach chooses sample sizes and allows the success rule used after testing to be distinct from the prior beliefs used to design the test. The authors illustrate it with demand data from emergency diesel generators and lifetime data from pressure vessels tested at different stresses. Their examples show that historical data and choosing how many units to test at each stress can raise assurance or reduce the required sample size.
narrate.key_results: For the generator example, the paper uses demand-test data from 63 generators; the resulting design posterior has a mean reliability of 0.990 and a median of 0.992. For 50 percent assurance using the design prior, the exact binomial, sceptical-prior, and mixture-prior methods require sample sizes of 227, 279, and 222, respectively; using the design posterior reduces these to 74, 141, and 78. For the pressure-vessel example, the authors analyze 87 failure times from 8 locations and set a target median reliable life of 4,000 hours at 25 megapascals. With equal allocation between two test stresses, 32 units achieve an estimated 80 percent assurance; an allocation of 20 units at 27 megapascals and 2 at 29 megapascals achieves 0.802 assurance with 22 units total.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The binomial model assumes independent, identically distributed outcomes, while the lifetime model relies on a common Weibull shape and a specified relationship between stress and lifetime; departures from these assumptions could affect the selected design. The examples use existing datasets and do not report prospective validation of the recommended test plans on new field or laboratory tests.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing free, open-source software and step-by-step guides for eliciting design priors. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess how other failure mechanisms, product covariates, and changing operating conditions affect assurance and stress allocation. It could also extend the design to system-level reliability and cost-based decisions, then validate the resulting plans prospectively with operational field data.

narrate.summary: Unexpected breakdowns of plasma etching equipment can cause production losses, while the equipment’s complex behavior is difficult to represent with one physical model. The authors train machine-learning models for three tasks: predicting time-to-failure (TTF), predicting a health score, and classifying whether failure will occur within a specified time interval. They use six months of operational data, including automatic process control (APC) sensor recordings, alarms, limit violations, equipment state changes, and voltage dips. They compare models with benchmarks representing simple and history-based human judgments, using four-fold cross-validation that keeps data from each interval between breakdowns together. The models generally outperform the realistic benchmark, with predictions more effective for longer horizons and alarms and limit violations among the most informative inputs.
narrate.key_results: For TTF regression on one chamber, linear regression (LR) using sensor and recipe features had an RMSE 36% lower than the realistic benchmark, 7% lower than the naïve benchmark, and 13% higher than the idealized visionary benchmark. In health-state regression, linear regression and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models outperformed all three benchmarks across the tested feature combinations. In interval classification, the best F1-score was 0.29 for the 0–8-hour interval versus 0.15 for its realistic benchmark, and 1.00 for the 14-day interval versus 0.64 for its benchmark. The authors report that prediction effectiveness was generally better for longer horizons, and conclude that models were acceptably effective for periods exceeding roughly 24 hours.

narrate.summary: This study examines whether changes in electrical resistance can warn of solder-joint failure before resistance thresholds are crossed. The authors analyze resistance measurements from nine electronic units as they undergo accelerated thermal cycling. They model warning signals using changes in memory in each unit’s resistance time series, measured with autocorrelation and detrended fluctuation methods. The resulting indicators are compared with conventional resistance thresholds and the eventual open-circuit failures. The authors find that the indicators generally provide earlier warnings, although the paper does not report a numerical prediction error or a quantified warning lead time.
narrate.key_results: All nine units failed after between 516 and 1,000 thermal cycles. The units began at about 0.008 ohm, making the triple-nominal threshold about 0.025 ohm; the other comparison threshold was a 20% increase above nominal resistance. The authors report that both early warning methods signal failure earlier than either threshold, and that the autocorrelation-based indicator warns earlier than the detrended fluctuation indicator in most cases. They do not give numerical accuracy, prediction-error, or warning-lead-time results.

narrate.future_work_unstated: A next step would be to validate the warning indicators on larger populations and field data under varied loads, temperatures, and other operating conditions, while measuring false alarms and useful warning lead time. narrate.summary: The paper addresses remaining useful life estimates that become unreliable when failures are rare, sensor readings are noisy, and many operating instances have not failed yet. It models remaining useful life as an ordinal prediction task using Long Short-Term Memory networks, and uses partial labels from right-censored instances during training. The authors also combine multiple independently initialized models and use the spread of their predictions to estimate uncertainty. They evaluate the method on the public C-MAPSS turbofan benchmark subsets FD001 and FD004, with simulated right-censoring of the training instances. The ensemble generally improves prediction results, with its largest reported gains over metric regression occurring when few failed training instances are available, and its uncertainty estimates tend to be lower for more accurate predictions.
narrate.key_results: With ninety percent of training instances treated as censored, the ensemble's root mean squared error was 20.38 on FD001, compared with 25.32 for metric regression, and 38.41 on FD004, compared with 41.23. The authors report these as improvements of 19.5 percent and 6.8 percent, respectively. In the uncensored comparison, the ensemble had root mean squared error of 14.62 on FD001 and 27.47 on FD004; on FD001 this was lower than the reported Long Short-Term Memory metric-regression result of 16.14, while on FD004 it was higher than the paper's own metric-regression result of 26.88. For instances with actual remaining useful life at most 20, the authors report uncertainty-evaluation precision of 0.917 on FD001 and 0.857 on FD004 using an uncertainty threshold of 0.2 and an error threshold of 10.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations list. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses only two simulated benchmark subsets, and the censoring scenarios are created by randomly truncating their run-to-failure records; the paper does not validate the approach on field data. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating semi-supervised pretraining with both failed and censored instances, and adapting the approach to non-stationary data. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the approach on field engine data and assess whether its uncertainty estimates remain reliable across operating conditions and failure modes not represented in these benchmark subsets. narrate.summary: The paper studies replacement when shocks add damage over time while a unit’s strength decreases. Failure can occur when a shock pushes accumulated damage beyond the unit’s strength, or when degrading strength falls below damage already accumulated. It models preventive replacement at a planned age, a shock count, or a damage threshold, alongside corrective replacement at failure, and seeks to minimize expected cost per unit time. Because exact calculations are difficult, the authors simulate damage, shock arrivals, and degradation, then use numerical search to select policy settings. They illustrate the method with data from 22 mailbox systems and 11 cell-phone batteries, as well as simulated examples with several damage and shock-arrival distributions.
narrate.key_results: For the mailbox data, with failure cost 2 and preventive replacement costs set to 1, the jointly selected policy was a replacement time of 708.89, a shock threshold of 183, and a damage threshold of 3.86, with an expected cost rate of 3.82 times 10 to the minus 3. For the cell-phone battery data, with failure cost 2 and preventive costs of 1, the jointly selected time and shock thresholds were 73.41 hours and 28 shocks, with an expected cost rate of 1.458 times 10 to the minus 2; the paper reports that the age-based policy performed better than the shock-count policy in this case. In one simulated example with exponential shock intervals and exponential damage, the directly calculated and simulated cost rates were 0.034 and 0.033, respectively, and their selected policy values were close. The simulation procedure used 10,000 realizations to estimate replacement times and replacement probabilities for a candidate policy.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the expected cost rate is not generally an exact long-run mean cost when shock arrivals do not restart after replacement; in that setting, they describe it as an approximation or as a measure for the first replacement. narrate.summary: The paper addresses the high computational cost and possible inaccuracy of reliability-based design optimization (RBDO), especially when reliability is assessed with approximate methods that can struggle with nonlinear failure boundaries or multiple failure regions. It proposes a general framework with separate blocks for adaptive surrogate modelling, reliability analysis, and numerical optimization. The framework is demonstrated using two analytical examples and a finite element model of a dome, with simulated model outputs rather than field data. The examples use surrogate models and Monte Carlo or subset simulation methods to estimate reliability while optimizing design. The authors find that the framework can produce solutions close to benchmark results while requiring relatively few evaluations of the original computational model.
narrate.key_results: For the first analytical example, framework configuration 3 produced a median optimized cost of 1.32 with 36.5 original-model evaluations, compared with a reference cost of 1.33 requiring about 10 million evaluations. For the short-column example, configuration 3 obtained a cost of 1.96 × 10^5 with 57 evaluations, compared with the reference cost of 1.96 × 10^5 and about 10 million evaluations. For the 16-dimensional dome problem, the optimized weight was 8.68 tons, using 154 finite element runs; validation with 1,000 simulated points found that the surrogate slightly underestimated the displacement quantile. Across the examples, the authors report that the framework was more efficient and robust than approaches based on first-order reliability approximations, while its results depended on adequate enrichment convergence.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstrations cover only three numerical examples, and the dome surrogate is validated against a limited simulated sample rather than independent field measurements. narrate.summary: This tutorial reviews how environmental contours describe combinations of extreme marine and coastal conditions and how engineers use them to estimate structural responses. It explains that a contour does not generally determine the failure probability or the response for the same return period without further assumptions. The authors describe joint environmental models and contour methods, then compare contour-based response estimates with direct simulation. Their case studies use significant wave height and peak period from a North Sea hindcast, together with simulated structural responses. They conclude that contours can be useful approximations in suitable cases, but response-based analysis is preferable when practical and contour results require careful checking.
narrate.key_results: The case studies use the NORA10 hindcast sample for 1979–2013 and compare contour-based estimates with direct simulation of 100-year maximum responses. Using points across the contour frontier, the estimated response quantile was 1% to 9% below the direct-simulation estimate across the four response examples. Using points near the contour location with maximum significant wave height produced scaling factors from 0.98 to 1.04, showing reasonable agreement in these examples but not guaranteeing it in other applications. In a comparison of contour types, direct-sampling and joint-exceedance contours agreed well on the relevant frontier, and the authors emphasize evaluating response at multiple points on or near that frontier.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the power Maxwell distribution (PMaD), an extension of the Maxwell lifetime distribution intended to provide more flexibility, including for data with a non-monotone failure rate. They compare the model with the Maxwell distribution and several related extensions. The authors report that the PMaD fits all four datasets better by the model-selection statistics they examined, and that Bayesian estimates are more precise in their simulation study when the prior is informative.

For sample size 10 and the stated parameter setting, the reported mean squared error for beta was 0.2588 for maximum likelihood and 0.2027 for the Bayesian estimate. Across all four real datasets, the PMaD had the lowest reported negative log-likelihood, Akaike information criterion, corrected Akaike information criterion, Bayesian information criterion, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic among the compared distributions. For example, on the bladder remission dataset, its Akaike information criterion was 736.7639, compared with 828.2464 for the extended Maxwell model and 2030.8870 for the Maxwell model.

narrate.summary: The paper develops objective Bayesian inference for a repairable system with several competing failure causes. narrate.key_results: In the two-cause simulation, the proposed estimate of the first shape parameter had a mean relative error of 0.9991 in scenario 1, compared with 1.2401 for the maximum likelihood estimate; for the second shape parameter, the corresponding values were 0.9980 and 1.5693. narrate.summary: The paper introduces the exponential-generalized truncated logarithmic (EGTL) lifetime distribution as an extension of the exponential-logarithmic (EL) model. It models the kth-smallest component lifetime when the system is assumed to fail after a specified number of component failures, rather than modelling only the first failure. The paper derives distribution, reliability, and failure-rate properties, and presents maximum likelihood, expectation-maximization, method-of-moments, and Bayesian estimation. The methods are evaluated with simulated samples and with brake failure times and yarn fatigue test data. The authors find that the model can represent increasing failure rates for k greater than 1, and that several fitted cases are consistent with the two datasets under the reported goodness-of-fit tests.
narrate.key_results: In simulations using 1000 samples at each of sample sizes 20, 50, and 100, the reported variances and mean square errors generally decreased as sample size increased; the Bayesian results were generally lower than the maximum-likelihood results. For the 107 brake failure times, the EGTL fit at k=2 had a Kolmogorov-Smirnov value of 0.0639 and p-value of 0.7746, while the Weibull fit had 0.0490 and 0.9999. For the 100 yarn fatigue observations, the EGTL fit at k=3 had a value of 0.0879 and p-value of 0.4218, compared with 0.0760 and 0.6080 for the Weibull fit. At the 5% significance level, the reported EGTL fits for k=2, 3, and 4 were not rejected for either dataset, whereas the k=1 fits were rejected, with p-values of 0.0000 for the brake data and 0.0009 for the yarn data.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses frequent corrective stops in sugarcane harvesters, which can interrupt production. narrate.summary: The paper addresses the high computational burden of estimating cascading blackout risk for many possible component maintenance choices. It uses simulation samples from a baseline system to estimate risk under changed component failure probabilities, without rerunning simulations for every maintenance strategy. The authors formulate selection of components for maintenance as a risk-minimization problem subject to a limit on the number maintained. They also estimate the sample size needed to meet a specified risk-estimation accuracy and propose two heuristic search algorithms. Tests use simulated cascading outages on 57-bus and 300-bus power-system models and show that selected maintenance can reduce estimated blackout risk.
narrate.key_results: In the 57-bus study, maintaining transformer number 7 reduced estimated risk by 2.8 percent for the zero load-shedding threshold, compared with a mean single-transformer reduction of 0.9 percent. Maintaining four transformers reduced risk by 3.5 percent for that threshold and by 6.2 percent at a load-shedding threshold of 200. In the 300-bus study, the selected strategy of maintaining eight transformers yielded a reported risk reduction of 21.5 percent; the estimated relative error fell from 41.9 percent at 5,000 samples to 9.7 percent at 95,000 samples. Sampling took 107 minutes, while the reported total computation times were 114.69 minutes for Algorithm I and 114.03 minutes for Algorithm II; in a 57-bus comparison, Algorithm II used 62 scenarios versus 2,380 for enumeration, but the heuristic was not always optimal.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of estimating blackout risk when component failure probabilities change, because conventional simulation must be repeated and cascading-outage paths can be numerous. It models cascading outages as a Markov sequence of system states and represents component failure probabilities with general component failure probability functions. Its method reuses paths sampled under an original set of failure probabilities and reweights them to estimate risk under changed functions, without running new outage simulations. The authors test the method with simulated cascading outages on a 300-bus power-system model, including 411 components. The reported calculations closely match estimates from newly run simulations while requiring far less computation across many changed-probability scenarios.
narrate.key_results: For a baseline of 100,000 simulated paths, the estimated blackout risks were 54.2 with no positive load-shedding threshold and 0.43 at a threshold of 1,500 megawatts. For changed component failure functions, the proposed estimates and estimates from 100,000 newly simulated paths were nearly the same in the reported comparison plots; the paper gives no numerical error measure. Lowering the minimum failure probability for component 204 reduced risk by 6.0 percent at the zero threshold, compared with a mean reduction of 0.2 percent across the single-component scenarios; at the 1,500-megawatt threshold, component 259 gave a 16.7 percent reduction, compared with a mean of 0.5 percent. Generating the baseline paths took 107 minutes, and processing 84,666 scenarios took about 10 minutes to calculate weights plus about 10 minutes for risk estimates, whereas the authors estimate that rerunning simulations for all scenarios would take about 9,000,000 minutes.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a data-driven framework for uncertainty quantification when engineering inputs have complex dependencies that independence or a Gaussian dependence model may not represent. It models input dependence with regular vine copulas, built from pairwise copulas, and combines the resulting model with existing response and reliability methods. The framework is demonstrated on two simulated finite element truss models with uncertain loads, using Monte Carlo simulation as a reference where feasible and fitting vine models to samples of 300 input observations. The authors find that modeling dependence accurately matters more than choosing a more advanced estimation method: Gaussian and independence assumptions can substantially misestimate response variability and structural failure probabilities.
narrate.key_results: For the horizontal truss, the reference failure probability was 5.04 × 10^-4 with the tail-dependent vine, compared with 0.15 × 10^-4 under independence and 0.34 × 10^-4 under a Gaussian copula. A vine inferred from 300 simulated input observations gave a Monte Carlo estimate of 3.30 × 10^-4, while the first-order reliability method estimate was 2.94 × 10^-4. For the dome, importance sampling estimated failure probabilities of 3.13 × 10^-5 for the specified vine and 3.27 × 10^-5 for the vine inferred from 300 observations; the corresponding independence and Gaussian estimates were 7.13 × 10^-3 and 2.47 × 10^-4. In the dome response-moment comparison, the standard deviation estimates were 1.164 mm under independence, 0.588 mm under the Gaussian copula, and 0.552 mm under the specified vine; polynomial chaos expansion worked with the vine model and converged faster than Monte Carlo simulation in the examples.

key_equations.name: Failure probability
key_equations.explanation: P_f is the failure probability, P is probability, Δ is the structural response displacement, and δ* is the critical displacement threshold.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that automated vine selection can become computationally prohibitive with many input dimensions or pair-copula families, and that selection remains an open problem in very high dimensions, which they characterize as greater than 50, or for very large samples. Computing the forward and inverse Rosenblatt transforms can also be computationally demanding or numerically unstable in these cases. Their framework is restricted to continuous input marginals, and inference uses the simplifying assumption that conditional pair copulas do not vary with the conditioning values beyond their arguments.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstrations use simulated inputs and two truss models rather than field measurements, so the accuracy of dependence inference with real, potentially noisy engineering observations is not established. The dome's rare-event estimates lack a reliable large-sample simulation reference, and the study does not quantify how errors in the chosen marginal distributions or vine structure affect those estimates.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further work to address computational challenges in vine selection and transformation, including the high-dimensional and large-sample cases. They note that prior information and Bayesian methods, grouping independent input subsets, and parallel estimation techniques could help with these challenges.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using monitored structural loads and field failure or displacement data, including tests of how sampling noise changes the inferred dependence and reliability estimates. Further studies could also incorporate changing operating conditions and load covariates, compare system-level failure criteria, and assess how reliability decisions change when dependence-model uncertainty is accounted for.

narrate.summary: Earthquake damage to bridges can disconnect transportation networks, while estimating the chance that two locations remain connected with repeated simulations can be computationally expensive. The paper trains two deep neural network (DNN) surrogates: a classifier that predicts connectivity for a sampled network, and an end-to-end model that predicts expected connectivity directly from roadway failure probabilities. It models earthquakes, ground motion, bridge damage, roadway failures, and network connectivity for the San Jose–Mountain View transportation network using simulated data. The simulations use a network with 39 bridges, 12 nodes, and 18 roadway links, and treat bridges as the only earthquake-vulnerable components. Both surrogates closely match the reference calculations, while the end-to-end model substantially reduces computation time.
narrate.key_results: For five fixed earthquake magnitudes, the classifier's binary accuracy ranged from 0.9995 to 1.0000 and it took about 0.62 to 0.65 seconds, compared with 5.23 to 6.05 seconds for exact depth-first search (DFS) checks. For a probabilistic earthquake event, the classifier estimated expected connectivity as 0.9001, versus 0.9002 using DFS, and took 53.89 seconds versus 603.97 seconds. When ground-motion residual variability was included, both methods estimated connectivity as 0.6853; classification accuracy was 0.9990, and the classifier took 53.08 seconds versus 574.48 seconds for DFS. In the end-to-end comparison, both approaches estimated connectivity as 0.9001, with reported computation times of 0.71 seconds for the surrogate and 7,857.92 seconds for the reference analysis; in the sensitivity study, selected bridge retrofit improvements were also closely matched.

key_equations.explanation: Here, Pc is the estimated expected two-terminal connectivity, N is the number of simulated network realizations, j indexes each realization, and g_j is 1 when the source and terminal are connected in realization j and 0 otherwise.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the end-to-end model is trained using classifier predictions rather than exact connectivity labels, so its training data are not exact, although they expect the resulting error to be negligible. For the end-to-end demonstration, they omit ground-motion prediction residual variability for simplicity.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers one relatively small, simulated transportation network and does not validate the surrogate against post-earthquake field observations or a larger range of network structures. Performance outside the simulated earthquake and failure-probability distributions is therefore uncertain, and the assumptions that bridges are the only vulnerable components and that the modeled failure process is adequate may limit transfer to other settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose augmenting the training data to improve classification specificity, including by generating additional known-disconnected network topologies. They also propose using graphics processing units to accelerate neural-network training and prediction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the surrogates on other infrastructure networks and field-observed earthquake damage, while adding non-bridge failures, additional operating conditions, and relevant network or hazard covariates. It could also extend the sensitivity demonstration to budget-constrained retrofit decisions and system-level service outcomes, and quantify uncertainty in surrogate predictions.

narrate.summary: The paper models damage that builds up in lumber under sustained and changing loads, which can reduce strength and eventually cause failure. It proposes a stochastic gamma process in which random damage within a piece is separated from the applied load profile and a population-level degradation function. The model is fitted using Bayesian analysis of failure-time data from 637 Western Hemlock pieces in three accelerated laboratory loading tests, including right-censored tests. It is also used to predict failure under a simulated 50-year residential load profile and to estimate remaining life for pieces that survive a test. The results show that the accelerated tests support wide uncertainty in long-term reliability estimates, and the gamma-process estimate of failure risk is higher than the estimate from the compared accumulated damage model.
narrate.key_results: The fitted model estimated a population stress threshold of 413 psi, but its 95 percent posterior interval was wide, from 43 to 642 psi, so a very low threshold remained plausible. For the simulated 50-year residential load profile, the estimated failure probability was 9 percent, with a 95 percent posterior interval of 5.5 to 15 percent; the compared accumulated damage model estimated 1.5 percent. For pieces surviving four years at 3000 psi, the 95 percent interval for the median remaining life was 21.9 to 333.5 years; after one year at 4500 psi, it was 5.2 to 24.3 years. The two-power time function fit the test data better than the simple power-law form, while predictions beyond the test durations remained highly uncertain.

key_equations.name: Load-dependent shape parameter
key_equations.explanation: Eta at time t is summed over m load thresholds, where t-tilde-i is the time exposed to at least threshold tau-i, a, b, c, u, and v are model parameters, tau-i is a load threshold, and the positive-part operator sets negative values to zero.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the accelerated tests, truncated at one and four years for the constant-load groups, leave substantial uncertainty in predictions over much longer periods. They also report weak evidence for a stress threshold and wide uncertainty in parameters governing longer-term degradation. They say larger or longer tests, or suitable expert knowledge in Bayesian priors, are needed to improve long-term reliability estimates.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The data come from laboratory tests on one visually graded Western Hemlock population, and the paper does not validate predictions against field failure histories. Long-term predictions depend on extrapolating the fitted time function far beyond the observed constant-load test durations and on applying a common parameter set across load scenarios. The model also assumes independent damage increments and does not jointly model moisture, temperature, or other environmental factors.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for larger tests or tests conducted over longer periods to reduce uncertainty in long-term predictions. They also identify moisture and temperature as potential additional degradation components, but say they lack data to demonstrate those extensions. They note that expert knowledge could be incorporated through the Bayesian priors.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The model could be tested on field data and on other lumber populations and engineered wood products, with operating conditions and specimen characteristics recorded as covariates. Further work could assess dependence between damage increments and competing failure mechanisms, then connect member-level predictions to system-level structural reliability and maintenance or inspection decisions.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a signature-based approach to redundancy allocation problems (RAPs) in coherent engineering systems. It addresses systems with heterogeneous component lifetimes and systems whose component lifetimes are dependent, and considers both active and standby spare components. The method transforms each candidate system into an equivalent system with independent and identically distributed (IID) component lifetimes, allowing system signatures and stochastic ordering results to be used in comparisons. The paper illustrates the approach with series systems and a five-component bridge system, using assumed lifetime distributions and dependence models rather than observed failure data. The examples show that the preferred spare location depends on component and spare lifetime distributions and, for dependent components, on their dependence structure.
narrate.key_results: For a two-component series system with one active spare, the paper recovers the result that placing the spare with the weaker component gives at least as good a system lifetime in stochastic order under the stated conditions. In the five-component bridge example with one active spare, the reported table selects component 4 for several listed sets of exponential rates, component 2 for other sets, component 1 for one set, and either component 1 or 4 for another. For a standby-spare example, the paper compares two policies using exponential, Pareto, and spare lifetime distributions and reports one policy as superior in stochastic order from the plotted equivalent-component reliabilities, even though a cited sufficient condition does not apply. In a dependent-lifetime example using a Clayton copula, the paper finds that one allocation is better in stochastic order if and only if the first component is weaker than the second under the stated assumptions.

key_equations.name: Signature representation of system reliability
key_equations.explanation: F̄_T(t) is the system reliability at time t, Σ is summation over positions i from 1 to n, s_i is the signature weight at position i, and Ḡ_i:n(t) is the reliability of the i-th order statistic among n equivalent component lifetimes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors emphasize that applying the method requires deriving the system signature. They also note that a reliability comparison may not identify an optimal policy in some cases, in which case another index such as mean time to failure (MTTF) may be used.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical illustrations use selected distributions and small example systems, with no validation against field failure data or operational spare-allocation decisions. The dependent-lifetime representation and comparisons rely on specified dependence structures, and the paper does not quantify how computation or signature derivation scales for large systems.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Test the allocation method on field data and larger engineering systems, including sensitivity to uncertainty in component lifetime distributions and dependence parameters. Extend the comparisons to additional failure mechanisms, changing operating conditions, system-level consequences, and cost or maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Bayesian estimation for a two-level step-stress life test when lifetimes follow a generalized exponential distribution with a shared shape parameter and ordered scale parameters. It uses the cumulative exposure model to relate lifetime behavior before and after the stress change, and imposes that the scale parameter at the higher stress is larger. The method uses importance sampling to estimate parameters and form credible intervals, and is extended to complete data and several right-censoring schemes. Evaluation uses simulated samples and a laboratory test of solar lighting devices. The authors also choose the stress-change time by minimizing the sum of posterior coefficients of variation.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 5,000 repetitions, mean squared errors generally decreased as sample size increased; for shape parameter 0.6 and stress-change time 5, increasing the sample size from 10 to 50 reduced the reported mean squared errors from 0.2177 to 0.0173 for the shape parameter, from 0.0061 to 0.0012 for the first scale parameter, and from 0.0758 to 0.0026 for the second scale parameter. The reported credible-interval coverage percentages were generally close to their nominal levels, and average interval lengths tended to decrease as sample size increased. For the solar lighting device test, the estimated shape parameter was 1.4434 and the estimated scale parameters were 0.1810 and 1.7921; the goodness-of-fit distance was 0.2070 with a p-value of 0.1212. With scale parameters 0.1 and 0.2, the selected stress-change time was 3.6 for shape 0.6 and sample size 20, and 13.4 for shape 1.5 and sample size 50.

narrate.summary: The paper studies lifetimes when an item can fail from either of two competing causes and testing ends under a Type-II hybrid censoring scheme. It assumes independent latent lifetimes with exponential distributions, but the usual maximum likelihood estimates can fail to exist when no failures from a cause are observed. The authors define estimates that always exist and develop exact-distribution, asymptotic, bootstrap, and Bayesian inference methods. They evaluate the methods using Monte Carlo simulations and an autopsy data set for radiation-exposed mice, with the original failure causes grouped into two. The proposed exact-distribution and bootstrap confidence intervals perform well in the simulations, and the authors report that the exponential model fits the example data adequately.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 5,000 repetitions for sample sizes of 10, 15, 20, and 30, with two censoring settings and cause-specific parameter values of 1 and 1.3. For sample size 10 and the lower censoring setting, the reported coverage was 95.86 percent and 95.16 percent for the exact-distribution-based intervals for the two parameters, compared with 93.30 percent and 92.90 percent for bootstrap intervals and 91.86 percent and 92.17 percent for asymptotic intervals. The paper reports that estimate bias and mean squared error generally decreased as sample size increased, and that Bayesian estimates using the non-informative prior performed better overall than the proposed estimates. For the mouse data, the estimated parameters were 0.07221 and 0.09284; a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance of 0.28107 with p value 0.1306 supported the authors' conclusion that the exponential model was usable for this example.

key_equations.name: Proposed cause-specific estimate
key_equations.explanation: Estimated lambda_j is the proposed estimate for cause j; D_j is the observed failure count for that cause; W is total exposure time; and j indexes the two causes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that assuming exponential latent lifetimes is restrictive and that the exponential distribution has serious limitations. They also describe independence of the latent cause-specific lifetimes as restrictive, while noting that this independence cannot be tested from these data without covariates.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The methods and simulations rely on independent, exponential latent lifetimes, so they may not represent dependent causes or lifetimes with changing hazards. The real-data illustration uses one transformed mouse data set, and its goodness-of-fit check pools lifetimes without cause labels. The exact confidence interval construction also relies on a monotonicity property that the authors could not establish theoretically, and they describe its computation as involved.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further work for cases where latent failure times do not follow exponential distributions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the methods with non-exponential lifetime models, cause-specific covariates, and operating conditions that change over time, and assess whether dependence between failure causes can be incorporated. Validate the resulting estimates and intervals against larger field reliability data, and extend the analysis to system-level decisions that use the estimated cause-specific risks.

narrate.summary: When a system fails and its cause is masked, engineers may not know which components failed before the system or which component caused its failure, making component reliability difficult to estimate. The paper models component lifetimes with a Bayesian three-parameter Weibull distribution and uses a Metropolis within Gibbs algorithm to estimate each component’s reliability. It allows different lifetime distributions across components and does not require equal masking probabilities, while assuming component lifetimes are mutually independent. The method is evaluated on simulated two-out-of-three, complex five-component, and bridge systems, and on observed failure times from 172 computer hard drives, 38 percent of which had an unidentified failure cause. In the simulations, the proposed estimates generally have lower mean absolute error than the nonparametric comparator, particularly for the bridge system.
narrate.key_results: For the simulated two-out-of-three system, the proposed method’s mean absolute errors for components 1, 2, and 3 were 0.0350, 0.0282, and 0.0259; the comparator’s were 0.1356, 0.0176, and 0.1332, respectively. For the five-component simulated system, the proposed method had lower error for components 1, 3, and 4, with errors of 0.0426, 0.0180, and 0.0381, while the comparator was lower for components 2 and 5. For the simulated bridge system, the proposed method had lower errors for all five components: 0.0384, 0.0758, 0.0976, 0.0365, and 0.0565, compared with 0.0671, 0.0936, 0.1193, 0.0505, and 0.1777. Across the broader simulation study, which used sample sizes of 50, 100, 300, and 1000 and masked-data proportions of 0.2, 0.4, and 0.7, the proposed method generally had lower mean error; the reported exception was component 2 in the two-out-of-three system, and the methods’ difference narrowed as sample size increased.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations section. They state that their model uses a three-parameter Weibull distribution and assumes mutually independent component lifetimes; their masking probabilities are taken not to depend on system failure time.
narrate.limitations_unstated: A Weibull model may not represent component lifetimes well when their true distributions have shapes outside the Weibull family, especially when reliability is extrapolated beyond observed failure times. The real-data example has no known component-level truth for checking estimation accuracy, and it uses a single hard-drive dataset; the paper also does not report computation time or assess sensitivity to the prior choices.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that the approach can be extended to other lifetime distributions or to a pure likelihood method. They also describe application to accelerated life tests as possible.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method with dependent component lifetimes and masking probabilities that vary with failure time, as well as with covariates and changing operating conditions. Testing on additional field data with verified component failure causes would help assess accuracy, while system-level decision studies could connect component reliability estimates to maintenance or design choices.

narrate.summary: Component reliability is difficult to estimate when system failure hides the failure times of other components, producing substantial censoring. The paper proposes a Bayesian method that estimates each component’s reliability in coherent systems using a three-parameter Weibull lifetime model. Its likelihood accommodates right-, left-, and interval-censored observations, and the method is intended for systems with varied structures and component lifetime distributions. The authors evaluate it in simulations of bridge and 2-out-of-3 systems and in a real study of first marijuana use among California high school boys. In the simulations, the proposed estimator generally has lower mean absolute error than the comparison estimator, with similar performance in a small number of cases.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 6 scenarios, 1,000 generated data sets per scenario, and sample sizes of 25, 50, 100, 300, and 1,000; component censoring ranged from 54.4% to 90.0%. The three-parameter Weibull posterior mean estimator (W3PM) had lower mean absolute error than the Bhattacharya–Samaniego nonparametric (BSNP) estimates in the reported comparisons, except that the methods behaved similarly for component 3 in scenarios 2 and 4; the proposed estimator’s performance improved as sample size increased. The authors prove posterior propriety for sample sizes greater than 1 under the stated family of non-informative priors, while noting that the posterior is not proper for a single observation with a failure. In the real data study of 191 boys, the estimated posterior mean time to first marijuana use was 15.05 years.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify the three-parameter Weibull lifetime distribution as their main modeling assumption. They note that the comparison nonparametric method avoids choosing a parametric family, whereas their method relies on the Weibull assumption.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Although the method does not require component lifetimes to be independent, the paper does not provide an explicit joint dependence model; it presents component-level likelihoods. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using the methodology for reverse engineering: Bayesian model-selection techniques could select among alternative reliability systems using mixtures of reliability estimates. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further research could model dependence among component lifetimes explicitly and test the method on operational reliability data with additional operating-condition covariates. It could also evaluate how component estimates support system-level maintenance decisions and reliability optimization.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces the sequential surrogate reliability method, which uses a radial basis function surrogate to estimate failure probabilities while reducing evaluations of an expensive computational model. Existing reliability approximations can lose accuracy when the limit-state boundary is highly nonlinear, and some adaptive surrogate methods concentrate accuracy locally without improving other regions. The method adds points where the estimated limit-state boundary meets a high-probability region, while a minimum-distance requirement discourages clustering. narrate.summary: This retrospective study examines on-orbit anomalies in electric propulsion (EP) and compares propulsion reliability in geostationary Earth orbit (GEO). Early in the study period, EP had higher anomaly rates than CP in GEO, but its recorded rates fell substantially after 2005. The authors conclude that post-2005 EP performed better than CP on the combined frequency and severity of anomalies, while noting that major anomaly rates were not statistically distinguishable.

The estimated time-to-anomaly distributions had a Weibull shape parameter of 0.86 for minor events and 1.14 for major events, which the authors interpret as patterns consistent with early-life and wear-out anomalies, respectively. The EP anomaly rate in GEO fell from 3.23 × 10⁻⁴ per spacecraft-day before 2005 to 9.14 × 10⁻⁶ afterward, a 35-fold decrease; before 2005, the overall EP rate was about five times the CP rate. After 2005, overall EP and CP rates were not statistically different, but EP had lower fatal and minor anomaly rates and a statistically indistinguishable major anomaly rate. Across the EP sample, spacecraft with gridded ion engines had 32.8 times the observed risk of an anomaly compared with Hall-thruster spacecraft; the 90 percent confidence interval was 6.2 to 172.4.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the poor efficiency that random-walk sampling can have when estimating very small structural failure probabilities. It develops Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling for Subset Simulation (SS), including a rejection-based approach and a barrier-bouncing approach for generating samples within intermediate failure domains. The method is tested using simulated examples: analytical limit-state functions, Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions, a random-vibration model, and a three-story frame model. Its results show that HMC-based SS is generally at least as accurate as the component-wise Metropolis-Hastings comparator, and that the rejection-based approach often improves efficiency for rare events. Barrier bouncing can achieve lower estimate variability in some cases, but its extra computation can make it less attractive unless the barrier-hit time is available analytically.
narrate.key_results: For the linear limit-state example with reliability index 6, the rejection-based HMC estimate was 0.98 × 10⁻⁹ with coefficient of variation 0.52, compared with 1.03 × 10⁻⁹ and 0.68 for component-wise Metropolis-Hastings; the exact probability was 0.99 × 10⁻⁹. Both methods used a similar number of limit-state evaluations: 8,668 for rejection-based HMC and 8,754 for component-wise Metropolis-Hastings. For the three-story frame example, rejection-based HMC estimated failure probability as 2.78 × 10⁻⁴ with coefficient of variation 0.33, compared with 2.81 × 10⁻⁴ and 0.41 for the comparator; crude Monte Carlo simulation reported 2.60 × 10⁻⁴. The standard-space comparisons used 1,000 samples per intermediate level and 500 independent simulation runs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that barrier-bouncing HMC with numerically determined hit times and directions is approximate because the resulting proposals are not strictly symmetric. narrate.future_work_unstated: The method could be assessed using field-informed structural data and operating conditions, including changing loads and material or environmental covariates. Further work could also test multiple interacting failure mechanisms and system-level reliability, and compare how the estimates support practical engineering decisions.

narrate.summary: This paper reviews three ways to estimate the thermal index of polymeric materials from accelerated destructive degradation testing data. The methods model how material properties decline over time as temperature changes, then estimate the temperature associated with a target time to failure. The authors compare a traditional polynomial and least-squares procedure with a parametric likelihood method and a semiparametric method that uses monotone splines for the baseline degradation path. They illustrate the methods with laboratory adhesive bond data and evaluate them in simulations using both correctly specified and misspecified parametric models. The simulations find that the parametric and semiparametric methods generally estimate the thermal index more precisely than the traditional method, and perform similarly to each other.

Under model misspecification, scenario 8 had root mean squared errors of 6, 4, and 5, respectively. Across the simulations, the parametric and semiparametric methods were generally comparable and usually had lower estimation error than the traditional method; more temperature levels and time points tended to improve precision.

The authors test the methods on simulated Gaussian-process functions and on a nuclear-storage criticality-safety example based on simulator outputs. Their main finding is that the method targeting missed-set size performs well against the compared sampling strategies, including in the reliability example.
narrate.key_results: In the nuclear criticality-safety example, after 75 total evaluations, the proposed strategy targeting expected false negatives had a median type II error 27% lower than integrated mean squared error sampling; the other conservative strategy was 25% lower, and the median for the non-conservative strategy was 12% lower. The true safe set occupied 88.16% of the input domain according to the paper's 50 by 50 evaluation grid. Across the synthetic benchmark, the two strategies designed for conservative estimates reduced expected type II error fastest in most tested batch settings, while adding space-filling points reduced the differences among strategies. The authors also prove that the expected type I error divided by the size of a conservative estimate is bounded by one minus the required inclusion probability.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for estimating the reliability and remaining useful life (RUL) of a running complex system when component failure data are scarce and may conflict with prior knowledge. narrate.summary: The paper addresses online detection of sudden anomalies in software-system performance signals, where seasonal trends and persistent correlations can make conventional detectors less reliable. For change detection, the paper reports that its ensemble outperformed the compared methods on the harder simulated task in equal conditions, while pretraining the subspace method made that comparator best on that task; on the easier task, the proposed method was slightly behind the cumulative sum procedure by area under the curve. narrate.summary: This paper proposes a statistical model for degradation measured across a spatial area over time. It addresses spatially different degradation rates, directional spread into neighboring areas, complex space-time dependence, and the computational burden of fitting large spatial models. The model represents degradation as generated degradation plus degradation propagated from prior observations through a spatial convolution. It is demonstrated using anonymized surface-scanner data arranged as a 21 by 21 pixel array and observed at times 1 through 20, along with simulated datasets. The fitted model represents the observed propagation pattern, and simulations are used to estimate when and where degradation may reach a threshold.
narrate.key_results: For the surface-scanner example, the Gaussian spatial covariance model matched the empirical variogram best among the three covariance forms considered. Under that model, the estimated decay parameter was 0.09, the estimated propagation vector was (-0.004, 0.793), and the estimated degradation-generation effect was 1.251; the reported 90% confidence interval for the second propagation component was (0.728, 0.857). In 500 simulated datasets, the authors describe the parameter estimates as having relatively small bias and report mean squared errors for all eight parameters, ranging from 2.86 × 10^-6 to 3.58. In a separate threshold simulation using 500 runs, the remaining useful life was most likely to fall between 4 and 8 time periods, and the first threshold crossing was most likely in one of the three high-degradation regions.

In the bridge-system example with later-than-expected failures, the authors report wider posterior system-reliability bounds over times 1–4.4, while the conflict is not of elevated concern for the whole system at mission times greater than 2.6. narrate.summary: The paper addresses estimation of transmission-line failure rates under specified operating conditions when outage samples are limited. It models hourly failure as a binary outcome and uses the imprecise Dirichlet model to estimate probability intervals for operational conditions given failure. A credal network combines those estimates with temperature, wind, rain, lightning, loading, and snow or ice conditions; line age is represented through a prior failure rate for lines of similar age. The authors report that its failure-rate intervals are tighter and more reasonable than intervals from two comparison methods, while representing estimation uncertainty explicitly.
narrate.key_results: For the two observed lines, the authors use 40 failure samples and report interval estimates for three operating scenarios. The estimated conditional failure-rate intervals are [1.85E−2, 2.38E−2] for an adverse-weather, high-loading scenario on the 5-year-old line; [8.88E−6, 1.94E−5] for a milder scenario on that line; and [2.85E−2, 3.66E−2] for the adverse scenario on the 10-year-old line. For a scenario with uncertain wind speed on the older line, the reported interval is [2.05 × 10−2, 2.65 × 10−2]. In a simulated study of 10,000 hours, with assumed failure rates of 0.0001 under normal conditions and 0.005 under adverse conditions, the authors report faster convergence and tighter, more reasonable intervals than the central-limit-based and chi-square-based approaches; they provide no numerical accuracy score.

narrate.summary: Accelerated destructive degradation testing (ADDT) uses harsh conditions to obtain degradation measurements sooner, but parametric models can fit poorly when their assumed degradation shape is wrong. The authors propose a semi-parametric model that uses a monotone spline for the degradation path and a parametric temperature relationship to support extrapolation to use conditions. The model and estimation procedures are evaluated using simulated data and three published laboratory datasets on adhesive bond strength, seal strength, and adhesive formulation strength. In simulations, the semi-parametric method was more robust to an incorrect parametric model, although it had greater variability than the correctly specified model. In the three applications, it fit the observed data well and had a lower Akaike information criterion than the corresponding parametric model.
narrate.key_results: In the misspecification simulation, the root integrated mean square error was 0.0091 for the semi-parametric model, compared with 0.0274 for the incorrect parametric model and 0.0043 for the true parametric model. For simulated mean time to failure (MTTF) at 30°C, the semi-parametric estimate had a mean of 82.77 and bias of 0.16, compared with a mean of 82.60 and bias of 0.01 for the true model and a mean of 85.82 and bias of 3.20 for the incorrect model. Across the three real-data applications, the semi-parametric model had lower Akaike information criterion (AIC) values: -67.4418 versus -61.9330 for adhesive bond B, -387.4909 versus -379.9814 for seal strength, and -311.9797 versus -309.9016 for adhesive formulation K. Estimated MTTF values at the stated use conditions and a 70% failure threshold were 306 versus 270 weeks for adhesive bond B, 127 versus 222 weeks for seal strength, and 92 versus 68 weeks for adhesive formulation K, with the semi-parametric estimate given first in each comparison.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method to estimate long-term maximum live-load effects when load magnitudes and event arrivals may be dependent. For a one-day maximum, the reported mean was 178.0 microstrain under the independent-observation assumption and 177.0 microstrain using the estimated dependence. For a 75-year maximum, the corresponding means were 574.4 and 570.3 microstrain. With an extremal index of 0.50, the reported means were 153.3 microstrain for one day and 546.1 microstrain for 75 years, illustrating the effect of stronger assumed dependence.

narrate.summary: The paper examines whether two discrete lifetime models are useful for industrial components whose lives are measured by solicitations or cycles rather than calendar time. The authors compare the models using simulated lifetimes and two industrial feedback datasets with substantial right-censoring. They find that the continuous Weibull model is a close practical substitute for W1, especially for reliable components and heavily censored data. narrate.key_results: In simulations, the authors generated 5,000 samples at each setting, with sample sizes of 50 and 100 and right-censoring rates from 0% to 75%; the mean estimation errors were close for W1 and the continuous Weibull model, with no significant improvement from W1. The first industrial dataset had 497 observations, 18 failures, and 479 right-censored observations; the second had 48 observations, 9 failures, and 39 right-censored observations. For the first dataset, W1 estimates were eta 306.814 and beta 2.320, compared with eta 320.580 and beta 2.320 for the continuous Weibull model; for the second, the respective estimates were 1530.139 and 1.122, compared with 1510.250 and 1.124. The fitted models gave similar failure-probability predictions over the observed ranges, but for the first dataset the IPD gave more optimistic predictions at higher solicitation counts.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the exponentiated Lindley geometric (ELG) distribution for lifetime data, motivated by the limits of models such as the exponential distribution, which has a constant hazard rate. The model compounds Lindley component lifetimes with a geometrically distributed number of systems and allows flexible hazard shapes. The authors derive distribution properties and estimate the three parameters by maximum likelihood, using an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm because the estimates have no closed-form solutions. They illustrate the model with relief times for 20 patients receiving an analgesic. In that example, the ELG distribution fits better by the reported information criteria than the Gamma, Weibull, and Lindley-geometric alternatives.

Its Akaike information criterion (AIC) is 37.1056, Bayesian information criterion (BIC) is 40.0928, and corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc) is 38.6056; each is the lowest among the four fitted models. The corresponding AIC values are 39.6372 for Gamma, 45.1728 for Weibull, and 42.6723 for Lindley-geometric. The likelihood-ratio statistic comparing ELG with Lindley-geometric is 7.5667, with a reported p-value of 0.0059; the paper also reports significant improvement over the Lindley model.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a hierarchical Bayesian method for estimating the reliability of individual components in series and parallel systems. It models each component lifetime with a Weibull distribution and uses gamma priors for the Weibull parameters, with prior means estimated by an Expectation-Maximization procedure. Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling produces posterior draws, which are used to estimate reliability and construct credible bounds. The method is evaluated using simulated data with right and left censoring, including data generated from Weibull, gamma, and log-normal distributions. The authors report generally good estimates of mean reliability time across the scenarios, while some results show bias under distribution mismatch and substantial censoring.
narrate.key_results: The simulation study covered 108 scenarios, each with 100 copies, using sample sizes of 30, 100, and 1,000, censoring proportions of 0%, 20%, and 40%, and true mean reliability times of 2 and 7. For log-normal-generated, right-censored data with a true mean of 2 and 40% censoring, bias and mean squared error at sample size 1,000 were 0.4371 and 0.1928, showing a remaining error under this condition. In a separate example with 100 systems and three components, the authors report that estimated component reliability curves were generally close to the true curves, although the true curves fell outside the 95% credible bounds over some short time intervals.
