narrate.summary: The paper introduces the exponentiated Weibull power series (EWPS) family to model failure-time distributions with more varied hazard shapes than a basic Weibull model. By combining an exponentiated Weibull lifetime with a power-series count distribution, it includes geometric, Poisson, and logarithmic submodels. The authors derive distribution properties and parameter estimation procedures, including an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. They fit the models to three real materials-test lifetime datasets: fatigue failures in two alloys and stress-rupture failures in Kevlar 49/epoxy strands. The results show that some EWPS submodels fit these datasets well, although the preferred fit varies by dataset and comparison criterion.
narrate.key_results: For 67 Alloy T7987 fatigue failures, the EWG model had a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0486 and a p-value of 0.9974; its Akaike information criterion (AIC) was 703.9917, while the EW model had a lower AIC of 702.0166. For 101 aluminum fatigue observations, EWG had the lowest reported Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, and Cramer-von Mises statistics among the compared models (0.0618, 0.3426, and 0.1299), while EW had a lower AIC (919.498 versus 921.1816 for EWG). For 101 Kevlar 49/epoxy stress-rupture observations, the authors report that EWG and EWP fit better than EW and Weibull by their comparisons, though the EWL and Weibull models have lower AIC values than EWG. The paper also derives that the family can represent increasing, decreasing, bathtub-shaped, and unimodal hazard rates; it reports no numerical prediction-error or reliability-cost results.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a Bayesian approach for estimating how component failure rates change with age when failure data are sparse. It models yearly failure counts using a piecewise homogeneous Poisson process, with candidate failure-rate trends including exponential, power-law, and bathtub-shaped forms. The case study uses operational failure and exposure data for electrical instrumentation and control components from 20 reactors of one reactor type, observed over 11 years and covering component ages from 1 to 15 years. The authors use Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo to estimate trend parameters and assess uncertainty about which trend model is appropriate. They find that model assessment criteria can disagree and demonstrate Bayesian model averaging as a way to include model-selection uncertainty in predictions.
narrate.key_results: The exponential model had the lowest deviance information criterion, at 86.48; the corresponding values were 88.00 for the Xie and Lai model, 88.42 for the power-law model, 91.39 for the linear model, and 94.00 for the generalized Makeham model. The posterior model probabilities were 0.422 for the exponential model, 0.216 for generalized Makeham, 0.147 for Xie and Lai, 0.108 for the power-law model, and 0.107 for the linear model. For all five models, the chi-square-based posterior predictive p-values were between 0.0042 and 0.0306, while p-values based on a standard-deviation discrepancy were between 0.5458 and 0.7356, illustrating that the two checks gave different assessments. The authors report a 95% predictive region for the next-year failure rate and describe the Bayesian model averaging region as narrower than the exponential-model region, but they provide no numerical prediction-error measure or forecast-validation score.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Lindley-geometric (LG) distribution, a two-parameter lifetime model formed by taking the minimum of a geometrically distributed number of independent Lindley lifetimes. Its hazard rate can decrease, increase, or have a bathtub shape, so it can represent several patterns of lifetime risk. The authors derive distributional properties and discuss parameter estimation by maximum likelihood, including an expectation-maximization algorithm. They fit the model to waiting times for 100 bank customers and to vinyl chloride measurements from environmental monitoring wells. The paper reports that the model fits these two data sets competitively against several standard lifetime distributions.
narrate.key_results: For the bank-customer data, the LG model has a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0567 and a reported probability of 0.9048; its corrected Akaike information criterion is 642, compared with 640.1 for the Lindley model. For the vinyl chloride data, the LG model has a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0800 and a reported probability of 0.9814, while its negative two times the log likelihood is 110.6, tied with the extended Lindley model. The LG corrected Akaike information criterion is 115 for the vinyl chloride data, compared with 114.7 for Lindley and 113 for the exponential model. Thus, the reported goodness-of-fit measures support the model as a competitor, but the tabulated criteria do not show it to be best on every measure.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a Bayesian sequential method for estimating the reliability of a parallel-series system. It models component outcomes as independent Bernoulli pass-or-fail results and places independent beta priors on their reliability parameters. The total test budget is fixed, while the tests are allocated sequentially among subsystems and their components to reduce the Bayes risk under squared-error loss. The paper uses theoretical derivations rather than data from an application, and it does not model degradation over time. It proves that the proposed hybrid two-stage allocation is first-order asymptotically optimal for the Bayes risk.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that, as the fixed total sample size increases, the risk multiplied by sample size converges to the stated limit in the equation below. The hybrid scheme allocates tests first among subsystems using estimated subsystem-level risk weights, then among components within each subsystem. This is a theoretical optimality result; the paper reports no numerical accuracy, prediction-error, failure-probability, cost, or empirical comparison results.

narrate.summary: The paper applies an enhanced Bayesian network to update reliability estimates as capacity measurements, load observations, and performance observations become available over time. It models a ductile frame with three failure modes and a hypothetical rail transportation network containing bridges and control systems. The numerical examples use specified probability distributions and constructed evidence cases, rather than field data. The method combines structural reliability calculations for continuous variables with Bayesian updating for discrete network models. The examples show that observations can substantially change reliability estimates and can guide replacement and measurement decisions, while computational complexity limits the size and detail of practical models.
narrate.key_results: For the frame with no measurement evidence, the reported reliability index is 1.94 and the failure probability is 2.6·10^-2; the corresponding Monte Carlo simulation check gives a reliability index interval of 1.93–1.94. With measurements M4=50 and M5=100 kNm, the model gives a failure probability of 0.24 and reliability index of 0.70, while the simulation interval for the index is 0.63–0.77; the other reported evidence cases also agree with simulation intervals. The value of information is 1,802 utility units for measuring R4, 1,168 for measuring R5, and 2,763 for both measurements together, so the preferred measurement depends on its cost. The life-cycle frame analysis required 19,251 first-order reliability method computations and about one CPU hour on the computer described in the paper, while subsequent updates took about one CPU second; infrastructure examples show that capacity measurements and observed component survival raise estimated reliability, whereas a large observed hazard can reduce expectations of future reliability.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses inaccurate prediction of software failure intervals with the Jelinski–Moranda reliability model, whose assumptions include independent, exponentially distributed times between failures. It proposes function-based nonlinear least squares estimation (FNLSE), which fits transformed observed and model-predicted intervals, and studies logarithmic and power transformations. The power-based method estimates the model parameters and selects its power index using recursively fitted data. The evaluation uses six standard benchmark software failure-time datasets from prior publications and compares the method with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), least squares estimation (LSE), and logarithm-based least squares estimation (LogLSE). All six datasets showed variance changing over time, and the power-based method with a selected index generally reduced relative prediction error, although its Braun-statistic results were mostly similar to LSE.
narrate.key_results: For the six datasets, the reported relative errors for power-based least squares with the selected index were 92.476%, 93.177%, 19.305%, 101.031%, 14.922%, and 706.623%, respectively; these were lower than the reported values for MLE, LSE, and LogLSE on every dataset. The corresponding MLE relative errors were 162.829%, 216.609%, 21.677%, 536.269%, 16.043%, and 2680.787%, while the LogLSE values were 125.966%, 150.135%, 21.224%, 208.453%, 16.230%, and 1511.177%. For the Braun statistic, the selected-index method improved on LSE for JDM-II (0.612 versus 0.847) and JDM-IV (0.918 versus 0.994), and matched LSE on the other four datasets. The authors report that all six datasets exhibited heteroscedasticity, meaning that their variance changed over time.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces RESID, a method for estimating software reliability while allowing debugging to be imperfect. Rather than counting bugs or measuring time between failures, the method estimates the probability that program chunks are buggy and uses program structure and chunk execution logs. After a detected bug is debugged, the model reduces that chunk's probability of remaining buggy by a known factor. The method is evaluated with simulated runs of a toy C program, not with field data. The simulations show estimates near the true bug probabilities across the tested settings.
narrate.key_results: In plots based on 100 simulated runs at true bug probabilities of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8, the log-likelihood peak was reported to be very near each true value. In 100 repetitions of 50-run simulations, for true probabilities 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9, the mean estimates across debugging factors 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9 were respectively 0.3269, 0.3161, and 0.3057; 0.6096, 0.6080, and 0.6155; and 0.9178, 0.9083, and 0.9006. The corresponding reported variances were 0.005, 0.003, and 0.002; 0.015, 0.010, and 0.006; and 0.009, 0.008, and 0.006. These are simulation results compared with the known probabilities used to generate the data; the paper does not compare RESID against another estimation method.

narrate.summary: Buckling strength in thin shells can degrade substantially because of geometric imperfections and uncertain material properties. This paper models buckling failure in a ring-stiffened submarine pressure-hull bay and optimizes its weight-related cost subject to a target failure probability. It uses an adaptive Kriging surrogate to estimate failure probabilities and guide optimization, with structural performance evaluated by finite-element simulations and a semi-numerical model. The inputs are simulated from specified probability distributions; the paper does not use measured field data. The authors find that reliability-based design optimization (RBDO) can explicitly control the accidental-depth safety target, while producing less cost-optimal designs than the worst-case approach.
narrate.key_results: For worst-case design, the finite-element-based cost was 0.1960, compared with 0.2004 for the semi-numerical model, a reported relative gain of 2% for the finite-element model. Under RBDO with target reliability index 6, the costs were 0.2356 and 0.2847, respectively, a reported relative gain of 17% for the finite-element model. The accidental-depth reliability indices were 6.06 and 6.11 for the two RBDO designs, compared with the target of 6; the paper states the target failure probability is below 10^-9. The adaptive procedure converged within 850 calls to the buckling-strength models, and one finite-element analysis took about 10 minutes on the authors’ computer.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses estimation of a failure or exceedance probability when a deterministic limit-state function is monotone in its inputs; it does not model degradation over time or lifetime data. The method samples inputs sequentially and uses monotonicity to identify regions known to be safe or failed, narrowing bounds on the probability. It then estimates the probability by maximum likelihood from the dependent sequence of failure-or-safe classifications. The method is examined theoretically and in simulated toy examples and a simplified hydraulic flood model. The paper finds lower estimation variability than ordinary Monte Carlo sampling under its assumptions, while also identifying finite-sample bias that it attempts to correct with a bootstrap based on monotone neural networks.
narrate.key_results: In the two-dimensional hydraulic example, the estimated probability was 0.002775; after 1,000 trials, the monotonicity-based estimate had a 0.12% coefficient of variation, compared with 60% for ordinary Monte Carlo and 27% for the first-order reliability plus importance-sampling method. At 200 trials, the corresponding coefficients of variation were 6% for the proposed method, 134% for ordinary Monte Carlo, and 44% for the first-order reliability plus importance-sampling method. In the four-dimensional hydraulic example at 1,000 trials, the proposed method had a 20% coefficient of variation, compared with 31% for ordinary Monte Carlo and 27% for the first-order reliability plus importance-sampling method. In toy examples, bootstrap bias correction was reported to be effective through dimension 5 with several hundred trials, and a budget of 1,000 trials was reported as sufficient for correction in dimension 8.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the technical assumptions needed for the theoretical results, although intuitively related to the limit-state surface, are difficult to verify in practice. They also say the bias-correction heuristic needs testing on more examples and further theoretical and applied study. They note that monotonicity may be a limiting assumption for high-dimensional structural-safety problems and point out that the cited practical examples do not exceed dimension 4.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The approach depends on global monotonicity in the transformed inputs, so a limit state with locally reversing effects or interacting failure mechanisms may not be represented appropriately. The demonstrations use simulated inputs and a simplified hydraulic model rather than field observations, so performance on real infrastructure data is not established; moreover, the neural-network bias correction and probability-bound volume calculations add computational work.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring support vector machines and constraints that make the predicted surface’s enclosed volume agree with the current estimate, as well as analytic bias correction and improved choices of which iterations to use. They also propose simplifying and classifying the theoretical assumptions, studying sensitivity to input distributions, developing better sequential sampling schemes, and adapting the method to partial monotonicity.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation on observed infrastructure or flood data, including comparisons across operating conditions and alternative input-dependence models. Further work could also combine partial monotonicity with multiple failure mechanisms and system-level reliability, then assess how the probability estimates support engineering decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper models total warranty expenditure over a fixed forecast period, rather than modelling an individual product lifetime or a particular degradation mechanism. In that case study, the normal cost approximation gave more convincing checks against the observed costs than the stable approximation, although the comparison uses only two observed periods.

The observed costs were 148,180.60 and 98,992.90, respectively. The authors' distributional diagnostic placed the first observed cost at cumulative probabilities 0.9981 under the normal approximation and 0.9998 under the stable approximation, and the second at 0.5649 and 0.9983; they judged the normal approximation better overall for these data, while noting that a single observation cannot establish distributional fit.

narrate.summary: Directly eliciting a joint prior for the Weibull lifetime model is difficult because experts may not be comfortable assessing its parameters. The paper proposes representing expert opinion as virtual lifetime data and calibrating the prior using an expert-specified lifetime percentile and a virtual sample size. It also describes how to calibrate prior uncertainty, combine independent expert opinions, and align priors when comparing Weibull and exponential models. The method is illustrated with two expert opinions about nuclear components and operational lifetime data that include right-censored observations. The results show that the approach produces tractable priors and makes the strength of expert information interpretable relative to the observed data, while also exposing when an expert opinion fits a Weibull model poorly.
narrate.key_results: For the two experts, the calibrated virtual sample sizes were 3.36 and 2.50; their calibrated prior mean shape parameters were 16.5 and 4.9, respectively, and the authors judged the first value physically unrealistic in this reliability context. The elicited credibility intervals were matched with less than 5% error across the considered virtual sample sizes, and the matching error at the calibrated sizes was below 0.2% and 0.004% for the two experts. The operational case contained 18 lifetimes, including 10 failures and 8 right-censored times; the maximum likelihood estimates of scale and shape were 140.8 and 4.51 months-based units, respectively. In the posterior analysis, the two expert opinions contributed relative information weights of 34% and 25% of the real-data information; for the second expert, the calibrated exponential-model virtual sample size was 6.70.

narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test calibration and predictive performance on larger, independent operational datasets across different component types and operating conditions. Further work could also incorporate covariates and competing failure mechanisms, and connect the elicited priors to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the exponential Poisson-Lindley (EPL) distribution for lifetime data with a decreasing failure rate. It models a lifetime as the earliest failure among an unknown number of defects, with each defect assigned an exponential lifetime. The authors derive distribution properties and estimate the two model parameters by maximum likelihood. The model fits both datasets reasonably well, but the reported comparisons do not show that it consistently outperforms established distributions.
narrate.key_results: For the airplane air-conditioning failure-time data, the EPL parameter estimates are 0.0101 and 0.9193; its Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is 0.1290 and its p-value is 0.6531. The exponential-geometric model has a slightly smaller statistic of 0.1262 and a larger p-value of 0.6793 on that dataset. For the vinyl chloride data, the EPL estimates are 0.4796 and 5.0811, with a statistic of 0.0882 and a p-value of 0.9331; the exponential-logarithmic model has a slightly smaller statistic of 0.0870 and a p-value of 0.9394. narrate.summary: The paper addresses prediction of remaining life for power transformers and forecasting the number of future failures in a utility fleet. Its data are complicated by units that entered observation after installation and by transformers still in service when records ended, producing left truncation and right censoring. The authors fit parametric lifetime distributions, stratifying transformers by manufacturer and installation period and using explanatory variables where supported by the data. They analyze 710 transformers with 62 recorded failures and use a random weighted bootstrap to calibrate prediction intervals for individual units and fleet failure counts. The method produces age-adjusted individual predictions and fleet forecasts; the authors report that the model's historical back-check agrees reasonably well with a nonparametric estimate, while results for newer units are more sensitive to modeling assumptions.
narrate.key_results: The Weibull model fit the data somewhat better than the lognormal model, and the final estimated Weibull shape parameters were 2.22 for the Old group and 5.01 for the New group. The fleet forecasts covered 648 transformers at risk, with pointwise 90% and 95% prediction intervals; the risk sets were 449 Old units and 199 New units. The authors also produced 90% prediction intervals for individual transformers, noting that some units had short intervals that indicated high modeled near-term failure risk. In a back-check using a 1994 data-freeze date to predict failures through 2007, the predictions agreed reasonably well with the Turnbull nonparametric estimates and lay within the reported 90% prediction bounds.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their prediction intervals account for statistical uncertainty but assume the statistical model is correct, so they do not include model uncertainty. The authors describe the fitted density and quantile plots as showing good fit in both examples, but do not report a numerical prediction-error measure or a numerical comparison against another model. They show theoretically that the hazard decreases when alpha is at most 1, while for alpha greater than 1 the hazard can take more varied forms.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a Gini-type coefficient to quantify how much a system ages or rejuvenates relative to a non-aging reference. It defines the coefficient for non-repairable systems using cumulative hazard and for repairable systems using cumulative event intensity. Positive values indicate increasing failure rates or event rates, while negative values indicate decreasing rates; values near zero indicate behavior close to the reference. The authors derive expressions for Weibull lifetime distributions and illustrate the measure for gamma distributions and several repairable-system processes. The paper is theoretical and uses numerical illustrations rather than observed reliability data.
narrate.key_results: The coefficient lies between negative one and positive one, and it is zero for an exponential lifetime distribution or a homogeneous Poisson process. For Weibull distributions and the corresponding power-law non-homogeneous Poisson process, the coefficient is one minus two divided by the shape parameter plus one, independent of the Weibull scale parameter. In the repairable-process illustrations over the interval from zero to two, the reported coefficients are 0 for the homogeneous Poisson process, 0.05, 0.33, and 0.50 for non-homogeneous Poisson processes with shape parameters 1.1, 2, and 3, respectively, 0.82 for a renewal process, and 0.21 for a generalized renewal process with repair effectiveness 0.5. The paper presents these as examples, not as comparisons based on empirical data.

Its numerical illustrations do not provide validation using field data, and the repairable-system definition focuses on increasing or decreasing event rates rather than explaining how to interpret a coefficient for non-monotone rates.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.

Further work could test its interpretation with field data across different failure mechanisms and operating conditions, and assess whether it supports system-level maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper studies software systems made up of modules that transfer control among one another. Incorrect module outputs can be catastrophic, or benign when the system can continue and recover; the model also allows a sufficiently long benign failure to become catastrophic. It derives system reliability expressions from a Markov model of these module transitions and from module testability. The proposed estimation procedure uses module test outcomes and transition counts, but the paper presents no empirical data. Its main result is a theoretical method for estimating system reliability, including systems that handle detected errors with safe outputs and resets.
narrate.key_results: The authors derive expressions for the probability of correct system completion in models with catastrophic failures alone and with both benign and catastrophic failures. They state that transition probabilities can be estimated by maximum likelihood and estimate overall reliability by averaging the estimated correct-output probabilities over tested inputs. The paper reports no numerical estimation accuracy, prediction error, or comparison of failure probabilities.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors acknowledge that assuming a benign failure becomes catastrophic after a fixed threshold departs somewhat from reality, although it simplifies the reliability calculation. They also say that application-specific knowledge would allow a more precise division between benign and catastrophic failures.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper gives no data-based validation, so it is unknown whether estimated transition probabilities or reliability represent operational software behavior. Reliability estimates also depend on the tested inputs being representative of actual use and on the modeled transition structure and failure classifications being appropriate.

narrate.summary: The paper considers reliability estimation for systems whose structural response changes nonlinearly as loading increases. It explains how a nonhomogeneous Markov chain can represent the evolution among discretized response states, offering an alternative to computationally intensive simulation. The transition probabilities are derived from joint and marginal response distributions, with normal distributions assumed for the states at successive stages. Failure probability is calculated by grouping states according to whether the response exceeds an allowable limit. The paper is a theoretical discussion based on existing literature; it presents no new data, numerical examples, or measured performance results.
narrate.key_results: The paper gives a method for constructing transition probabilities from the joint distribution of response at successive loading stages and the response distribution at the current stage. It describes calculating the probability of failure by summing the probabilities of states beyond the allowable response limit. It also presents a state-space distance based on overlap between probability distributions and argues that reversible system evolution preserves this distance. No numerical accuracy, prediction error, or comparison with another method is reported.

key_equations.name: Failure probability
key_equations.explanation: P_f is the failure probability, Y_k is the loading stage indexed by k, i indexes response states, k_1 is the last index of the states grouped as safe, and p_i is the unconditional probability of state i at loading stage Y_k.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors caution that the choice of probability densities used to calculate transition probabilities requires care. Their formulation assumes normal response distributions at individual loading stages and bivariate normal distributions across successive stages, and the paper provides no examples because examples are available in cited references.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Because the paper presents no numerical or field validation, it does not demonstrate whether the assumed distributions or state discretization represent actual structural responses well. The reliability calculation also depends on choosing an allowable response threshold and grouping states around it, but the paper does not assess how sensitive results are to those choices.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify further study of the quantum interpretation of statistical probability as relevant to future developments in experimental mechanics. They state that studies in this direction are being carried out at the Structural Engineering Research Centre.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The method could be tested against measured structural response and failure data, including checks of the normal-distribution assumption and the accuracy of estimated failure probabilities. Further work could also examine alternative response distributions and state partitions, and evaluate how the method performs as the number of states and loading stages grows.

narrate.summary: This review examines how expert judgement can support reliability assessment throughout the design and life cycle of engineered systems. Reliability estimates can be uncertain because future design, production, usage, maintenance, and system changes affect performance, while historical data may not represent a new system well. The paper describes how experts can help define failure modes, structure models, estimate uncertainty, and revise assessments as system-specific observations become available. It discusses expert judgement alongside historical and generic reliability data, and reviews methods used across design, manufacturing, operation, and maintenance. Its main message is that reliability assessment should be treated as a continuing feedback and decision-support process, not just as estimation of an unknown distribution.
narrate.key_results: This is a review paper and does not report new numerical estimates, prediction errors, failure probabilities, or cost comparisons. It surveys elicitation methods, reliability models, and stakeholder roles across the systems engineering life cycle. It argues that design problems require particular attention to qualitative model structuring and to uncertainty about future decisions, beyond approaches focused on precisely defined events. The authors conclude that a whole-life framework should track changing assessments and support agreement among stakeholders about uncertainty.

key_equations.name: Reliability as a function of system choices
key_equations.explanation: The symbol r is the chosen reliability measure, while d, p, u, m, and c represent choices for design, production, usage, maintenance, and changes.

key_equations.name: Tolerance uncertainty in failure rate
key_equations.explanation: The symbol lambda is the failure rate as a function of factor choice e, and E is the design envelope over which the minimum and maximum rates are considered.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that there is little published evidence on how effectively and efficiently standard qualitative reliability methods are applied, and no known scientific survey of their use. They also identify limited reporting on how elicitation should support test design and note that uncertainty in priors and model choice can compromise Bayesian updating.
narrate.limitations_unstated: As a review, the paper does not set out a systematic search and screening method or a reproducible basis for selecting the literature discussed. It does not empirically test the proposed whole-life approach against existing practice, so its practical benefit and resource requirements remain unmeasured.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for new elicitation methods and modeling tools that support systems engineering design, including holistic tracking of reliability assessments across the life cycle. They also identify the need to structure models as engineering understanding develops and to support rational consensus among stakeholders.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to apply a common whole-life elicitation framework to multiple engineering projects and assess its calibration, decision impact, and effort against current practice. Further work could also validate how uncertainty changes across operating conditions and stakeholder groups using field data from systems after deployment.
